bio.en: Nikhyl Singhal has led large consumer and product teams at Google, Facebook, and Credit Karma, and is a former VP of Product at multiple influential companies.
bio.zh: 尼基尔·辛哈尔（Nikhyl Singhal）曾在 Google、Facebook 和 Credit Karma 领导大型消费级与产品团队，并担任过多个具影响力公司的产品副总裁。

summary.en: Nikhyl uses the "fake rabbit" dog-track analogy to warn against defining success only as a future title or milestone, after which motivation dies. He urges planning for what comes next - a second act - so your career stays purposeful. The episode is a thoughtful take on long-term career motivation and avoiding the post-achievement void.
summary.zh: 尼基尔用赛狗场上"假兔子"的比喻警告：若把成功仅仅定义为未来的某个头衔或里程碑，一旦达成，动力便会枯竭。他敦促人们规划"下一步"——即第二幕——让职业生涯始终保持意义。本期是对"长期职业动力、避免成就后的空虚"的深思。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: When I was a kid and I was growing up in the Midwest, entertainment was like going to the dog tracks. The way that they motivated the dogs was they had these fake rabbits. These tails would go around faster than the dogs, which would then motivate the dogs to go around in circles. And what was interesting is the moment that the dogs, if they accidentally touched the rabbit, they would never run again because there was like, "Well, what's next? I've achieved what I was looking for." So I think this happens a ton, it's like your listeners are spending time focused on like, "Well, one day I will be X. I will be that vice president. I will have more money. I will have built something. I will have started a company." But they don't think about what happens next. What's the second thing? What's your career next look like? How do you ensure that you are always going to have something important and motivating to do with your career? Otherwise, you'll keep working because you know nothing else to do, but you'll be sadder or you'll find ways to create war when peace is needed.
turns.zh:
回想我童年在美国中西部成长的时光，娱乐活动通常是去赛狗场。那里用来激励狗狗的道具是假兔子玩具。这些兔子尾巴旋转的速度比狗狗跑得还快，这能促使狗狗开始追逐尾巴玩耍。有趣的是，一旦狗狗不小心碰到兔子尾巴，就会从此不再追逐，因为它们会想：“接下来该做什么呢？我已经达成了目标。”  

这种现象在职场中也很常见。比如听众们总会花时间专注于“未来某天我要成为X，成为副总裁，赚大钱，或是创立公司”，但却忽略了接下来的步骤：职业生涯的下一步是什么？如何确保自己的职业生涯始终充满挑战与动力？否则，你只能为了打发时间而工作，结果要么越陷越深，要么在本该和平共处的环境中制造矛盾。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Nikhyl, welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: 尼基尔，欢迎做客本期播客。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal

turns.zh: 谢谢你，莱尼。很感激能有机会参与。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I have a very simple question to start. How many product managers have you been a mentor to if you had to put a number on it?
turns.zh: 首先我想问个简单问题：如果要给出一个数字，您指导过多少位产品经理？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Good question. I guess I haven't thought about it from that perspective. I would say hundreds is probably the way to sort of answer the question, and a little bit has to do with whether how we define being a mentor. I know that was supposed to be a simple question and I'm going to give you a complicated answer, but I think that I started out just helping people 10, 15 years ago, trying to help them through their careers. I find the whole area really interesting. And then what happened was just I started to scale because people were always like, "Hey, can you find time?"
turns.zh: 好问题。我没怎么从这个角度考虑过。我觉得可能有几百位吧，这还是个粗略数字，而且这取决于我们如何定义导师的角色。我知道这应该是个简单问题，但我还是要说得复杂点。我最初只是帮助人们度过职业生涯中的难关，10年、15年前开始做这件事。我发现这个领域非常有趣。后来随着需求增加，人们总会问：“嘿，你能抽出时间吗？”

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: So now what I do is I tend to help and coach hundreds of folks through transitions. So if they're in a moment where they're trying to decide between another job, if they're trying to decide to leave, if they're having sort of an alert at work, I call them 911 calls. I take a few 911 calls every week and from a relatively large group of people. So I find those are the most substantive times to help people, is when they're in moments of dilemma or forks in the road, and that's why the number is more closer to hundreds.
turns.zh: 如今，我的工作是帮助数百人度过职业转变期。比如，当他们在犹豫是换工作还是离职时，当他们在工作中遭遇危机时，或者当他们面临人生十字路口时，我都会接到他们的"求助电话"。我每周都会接到不少这样的求助电话，这些人来自一个规模相当大的群体。我发现，在人们陷入困境或面临抉择的时刻，帮助他们最有意义——这也是我每周接到数百个求助电话的原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Follow-up question: How many of those people you've mentored have been on this podcast?
turns.zh: 好的。追问一下：你指导过的这些人中，有多少上过这个播客？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Probably half dozen to kind of close to a dozen at this point.
turns.zh: 目前大概有五六个，接近十个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow.
turns.zh: 哇，真不少。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah, easily half dozen.
turns.zh: 是的，至少五六个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay. Is there any names you want to name or should we keep it anonymous?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，那你是否介意透露他们的名字，还是希望匿名？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah. We'll keep it anonymous because I want people to feel they can always call me in and not feel like that. I don't tend to share the names of most people.
turns.zh: 是的，还是保持匿名吧，因为我希望大家能安心找我咨询，不必有顾虑。我一般不会透露大多数人的名字。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I know the one person that self-identified was Annie Pearl from Calendly, who is a big advocate of the stuff that you do. So we don't want-
turns.zh: 好的。我知道有个自述的嘉宾是来自Calendly的Annie Pearl，她可是你工作方法的忠实拥趸。所以我们不必——

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah. Annie is someone I learned from and helped talk with, and she's also part of a community that I also build on the side where we pulled a bunch of CPOs together and they've been building community. I'm a big fan of community and learning, and she's part of that as well.
turns.zh: 是的。Annie是我学习过并交流过的人，她还参与了我创建的一个社区，我们汇聚了许多首席产品官，共同构建了一个社区。我非常重视社区和学习，而她也是其中的重要成员。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I definitely want to talk about that, but maybe just set a little context for our conversation. I feel like you're in the very high percentiles of people that have seen a variety of careers in product management, both good careers, bad careers, junior people, senior people. So I want to focus most of our time on talking about just the PM career path and what you've learned about what is important to have a successful, thriving, happy PM career. Does that sound good?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我很想深入探讨这个话题，但或许先为我们的对话做个铺垫。我觉得你属于产品管理领域见多识广的少数人之一，经历过各种职业生涯阶段——无论是成功的还是不成功的，初级还是高级职位。所以我们大部分时间将聚焦于PM职业发展路径，以及你对如何拥有成功、充实、快乐的PM职业生涯的深刻见解。这样安排可以吗？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Perfect.
turns.zh: 完美。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So I'm thinking we break up the chat into early career, mid-career, and late career. So within the early career section, you've talked about how people often make a mistake in their early career, specifically being very short-term focused in deciding where they're going to go. And that's a very dangerous way of thinking about it. So I'd love to hear just your take on exactly what does that mean, and why is that actually a bad idea?
turns.zh: 好的。我打算把对话分成三个阶段：初期职业、职业中期和职业后期。在初期职业阶段，你提到人们常犯的一个错误是过于关注短期目标，比如急于决定去向。这其实是个危险的思维模式。能否请你详细解释一下这种短视思维的危害，以及为什么这是不明智的？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah. I tend to be long-term focused in most of my counsel, and maybe to give you an example of what a short-term focus career kind of framework looks like is, "I really dislike my boss. I feel like this company doesn't have it anymore. There's just too hard to ship things." Those are all maybe true statements, but they probably exist in many of the jobs that one would consider if they were to move for one to another. Lateral moves are by definition not forward moves. So what I try to tell people to think about is work backwards from your end state.
turns.zh: 是的。我在大部分咨询中都倾向于采取长远视角。举个例子说明短视思维的框架："我真的很讨厌我的老板。我觉得这家公司已经没救了。产品交付太难了。"这些可能是真实的感受，但在换工作时，这些抱怨在很多职位上都可能出现。横向跳槽本质上不是进步。我的建议是倒推终点。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Almost think of career as a product. So if you're building a good product, you think about, "Well, here's what a great product would look like," and then you break it into version one, version two, version three. Well, in some ways the reason I called my newsletter, my podcast The Skip is because I always think about not the next job, but the one after it. Maybe think about not your boss's job but your boss's boss's job and what do I need to think about to get there. And in many ways you may think, "Well, okay, if I need to found a company one day and that's my job after next," then you want to look at maybe your current job and then maybe the next job in service of that. And that may lead you to saying, "Hey, maybe I need a grit of doubt and maybe I should stay and maybe I should learn how to deal with some of this ambiguity. That's why I want people to be a bit more longer term and not so short-term focused.
turns.zh: 我几乎把职业生涯视为一个产品。所以如果你正在打造一款优质产品，你会想：“嗯，一款出色的产品应该是什么样子的？”然后你会把它分解成版本一、版本二、版本三。在某种程度上，我之所以把我的新闻通讯和播客命名为《The Skip》，是因为我总是在思考的不是下一份工作，而是再下一份工作。也许你不会只考虑老板的职位，而是老板的老板的职位，以及要如何才能达到那个目标。许多人可能会想：“好吧，如果我需要创办一家公司，而那是接下来要做的工作”，那么你就需要审视当前的工作，甚至是下一份为此服务的工作。这可能会让你产生疑惑：“或许我需要多些耐心，或许我应该留下来，或许我需要学会如何应对一些不确定性。”这就是为什么我希望人们能更着眼长远，而不是急功近利。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are some other examples of that short-term thinking? You talked about "my manager sucks, things are moving really slowly." What other examples where people maybe like, "Oh, okay, I see, this is actually short term. Let me think longer term"?
turns.zh: 还有哪些短期思维的例子呢？你提到过“我的经理很糟糕，事情进展太慢。”还有哪些情况下，人们会意识到“哦，原来这只是短期思维。我需要更长远地考虑。”

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I'd say the biggest one in workplace is focusing career and promotion together. I think that there's perhaps a light connection between promotion and career addition, but I feel like too many people are, the moment we talk about career, they're like, "Well, let me talk to you. I want to have a career talk with you." And I said, "Sure, why don't you find some time?" We sit down together and they're like, "Well, what do you think I need to do to get to promotion?" And then I said, "Well, promotion is our system at this company to see you moving forward. And it's pretty clear in terms of levels and what you're doing and what the process is and who makes the decision." And that's pretty short term because you can ask, "Hey, it's two years away, how do I make it 18 months?" It's a classic.
turns.zh: 我认为职场中最大的问题是将职业发展和晋升机会混为一谈。我觉得晋升和职业发展之间或许有某种微弱的关联，但太多人一提到职业发展，就问：“好吧，我想和你聊聊。”我说：“好啊，你找个时间吧。”我们坐下来后，他们会问：“那要怎么做才能晋升呢？”然后我会说：“嗯，晋升是我们公司的晋升体系，用来衡量你的成长的。晋升体系在层级、职责和流程方面都非常明确，由谁来决定也很清楚。”这就是典型的短期思维，因为你可以问：“嘿，还有两年时间，我怎么能缩短到18个月呢？”这太常见了。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: But in reality, if you're thinking career, you're thinking about the sort of long term arc and, as I said, maybe the job after next, and then you need to look at the promotion in service because how many people have you and I talked to who said, "Well then, as soon as I get promoted, I'm going to leave"? So then I'm like, "Well, okay, then what's the promotion in service of?" And you get into that conversation, which tends to be, again, very long-term focused.
turns.zh: 但实际上，如果你在思考职业发展，你应该着眼于长期规划，正如我所说，或许是再下一份工作，然后你需要审视晋升机会如何为此服务。因为我们聊过的很多人都说：“好吧，一旦晋升，我就离开。”然后我就问：“好吧，那晋升是为了什么？” 接着我们会深入探讨，而这种探讨往往又非常注重长远规划。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This makes me think about this interesting two-sided challenge with thinking about your future career and where you want to go. On the one hand, it's valuable to think about getting more logos in your resume and working at Netflix and Meta and Airbnb and Uber, all these guys, there's power and value to that. On the other hand, you just keep doing that. And then what is your life turning into? You're just chasing more fancy logos and feeling better about better brands and your resume and stuff. This might be too big a question, but just how do you advise people to think about how important it's to get some of these companies in your resume and build that side of it versus just doing things you actually enjoy and having a fulfilling life and doing things that are meaningful to you?
turns.zh: 这让我思考一个有趣的双重挑战：思考未来的职业发展和想去的地方。一方面，在简历上多些大公司的标识、在Netflix、Meta、Airbnb、Uber等公司工作，这些都很有价值。另一方面，你会一直做这些事。然后你的生活会变成什么样？你只是在追逐更多光鲜的标识，对更好的品牌、简历之类的东西感觉良好。这个问题可能太宏大了，但你如何建议人们思考在简历上获得这些公司的经历有多重要，以及如何在这一方面下功夫，而不是只做自己真正喜欢、能带来充实感和意义的事情？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah. I mean I think collecting labels does feel shallow to most builders because if you're a product person, you probably got into the business because you like building stuff. And frankly, not just product people want to do that, a lot of technical people want to just build stuff. And then the question is, is the things that you're working on in service of building? And then when you ask people, "Were you happy?" as they always say, "Well, when I was able to build this thing," and oftentimes they don't care whether it worked or not, which is kind of ironic. So for me, when I see people chasing logos, I think about it as well. I'm actually really a big fan of a diverse set of experiences, that I think learning about pre-product market fit then seeing smoke turn into fire and witnessing and maybe shepherding that and then taking fire and turning it into something great and being an experience set where you can see the movie in these different frames makes you just a better builder.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得对于大多数产品开发者来说，收集职位头衔确实显得有些肤浅，因为如果你热爱产品开发，可能最初选择这份工作就是因为喜欢创造东西。说实话，不只是产品经理想做这件事，很多技术人员也渴望能专注于开发工作。关键问题在于，你所做的工作是否能真正助力产品落地？当你问别人“你开心吗？”时，他们通常会回答：“嗯，当我成功开发出这个功能时。”但很多时候，他们并不在意产品是否真的成功了，这真是有点讽刺。所以当我看到人们追逐头衔时，我也会深有感触。事实上，我非常推崇多元化的职业经历——从了解产品市场匹配度到见证创意转化为现实，再到亲手将火种培育成熊熊烈火——这种全方位的视角能让你成为更出色的产品创造者。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: So you can't really go wrong if you're looking at those experiences. And you're looking at inside the building problems and outside the building problems, those are maybe consumer problems and business-to-business problems. The more diverse career you have, the better builder you are. And that usually comes up being satisfied. But the idea of just doing that because you think it's going to make your chances better for the next job maybe scares me and it feels very much in service of some future dream that is not build oriented. And I think that can be leading to sadness.
turns.zh: 所以只要你专注于这些经历，就很难出错。无论是处理产品开发中的难题，还是应对市场外的问题，比如消费者需求和B2B挑战，多元化的职业经历都会提升你的能力。而这种能力通常会转化为满足感。但如果仅仅为了下一份工作而追逐头衔，可能就有些本末倒置了。这种做法更多是为未来某个与产品无关的梦想铺路，我觉得这很危险。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that advice, and I say this often actually on this podcast, the power of a diversity of experiences for so many reasons. Maybe just to close this loop, would you agree there is a lot of value in having one of these FAANG ish companies on your resume? Like a lot of opportunity gets unlocked if you work at one of these companies that people are like, "Oh wow, okay, this person's interesting." Or not? Or do people maybe overthink that?
turns.zh: 我很赞同这种观点，事实上我常在播客中强调多元化经验的价值。说到这里，你是否认同在简历上写上FAANG（Facebook、Amazon、Google、Netflix、Apple）这样的公司经历很有价值？比如，如果你曾在这些公司任职，人们会觉得你很有趣，机会也会随之而来？还是说人们对此过于在意了？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Generically, the answer is yes. I think it's especially important for executives. I think that many executives are hired because they are to bring expertise of the next phase of organization to this company. We're growing, we want to go after the next phase. We want someone who's has expertise. The MAGMA or FAANG companies, however you want to describe them, they really have challenges and expertise at how to build things at scale, how to manage millions or billions of users and customers. So the advantage is, to be successful at that is an endorsement. Having said that, those specific companies, experiences can be substituted for other later stage companies, but if you're coming in as an executive to bring someone to the next level and you've never experienced it, it's very difficult thing to get that executive experience and to be like a C-level for that growth company.
turns.zh: 总体来说，答案是肯定的。我认为这对高管尤其重要。许多高管之所以被聘用，是因为他们能为公司带来下一阶段的组织管理专长。我们在发展壮大，想要开拓新领域，需要有专业能力的人才。无论是MAGMA还是FAANG公司（你可以随意称呼），它们在大规模产品开发、管理数百万乃至数十亿用户和客户方面都面临挑战。因此，成功应对这些挑战本身就是一种认可。话说回来，虽然FAANG不再准确（Facebook现在叫Meta），但MAGMA这个术语更贴切。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To point out, FAANG is no longer accurate because Facebook is now Meta. So MAGMA is the term that you prefer.
turns.zh: 我更偏爱MAGMA这个称呼。遗憾的是，这个术语排除了Netflix，但也未能涵盖Adobe、Salesforce等其他优秀公司。所以我觉得——

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I prefer that. I think it unfortunately kicks out Netflix, but it also doesn't pay homage to Adobe and Salesforce and a number of other great companies. So I think-
turns.zh: 我更倾向于MAGMA这个术语。不过它把Netflix排除在外了，这对Netflix来说不太公平，但也确实没法同时兼顾Adobe和Salesforce等其他优秀公司。所以我觉得——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: FAANG doesn't. Okay, I like this. Okay, let's try to make MAGMA the new thing. MAGMA, make that the title of this episode. Just joking.
turns.zh: 脸书、亚马逊、苹果、网飞和谷歌（FAANG）可不这么认为。好吧，我喜欢这个说法。好的，让我们试着把“MAGMA”变成新的热门话题。MAGMA，就让这成为本期节目的标题吧。开玩笑的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the next area I want to touch on is, you wrote this kind of hot take on something you call ex-growth companies and how it's not good to be at an ex-growth company currently. So can you just talk about what is an ex-growth company and then why is that not a good place to be as a product manager for probably any kind of role?
turns.zh: 接下来我想探讨的领域是，你写了一篇关于所谓“前增长型公司”的热门评论，指出目前在这样的公司工作并不理想。那么，你能否先解释一下什么是前增长型公司，以及为什么对于产品经理来说，无论处于何种职位，在这类公司工作都不是明智之选？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I have a pretty strong opinion on this that I think that for 10 years we created the hypergrowth, blitzscaling type phenomenon, and there was a lot of good reasons for that, some of which were just distribution platforms just got so good. You could take out Facebook ads, you could grow with Google, and you could grow in 18 months that maybe took previous companies 10 years. So I think that the idea was that all of these companies could instantly grow when they found product market fit and that birthed all these unicorns. And then suddenly, 18 months ago, it almost like the music stopped. 0% interest rate went away, and it became a lot harder to find growth through just fueling it with capital. And I think that the sudden change meant that not only capital was harder to raise, but companies started to focus on their core products. You've talked about it on this podcast, just how many layoffs and restructuring and managers moving to ICs, and all of that work is happening.
turns.zh: 我对此有很强烈的看法。我认为过去十年，我们创造了超高速增长、快速扩张的商业现象，这背后有诸多合理因素，其中之一就是分发平台的飞速发展。你可以投放Facebook广告，借助谷歌平台快速增长，可能只需18个月就能完成其他公司需要10年才能达成的目标。因此，人们认为只要找到产品市场匹配点，所有这类公司都能实现瞬间增长，由此催生了大量独角兽企业。但18个月前，突然间，增长引擎仿佛停摆。0利率政策消失，仅靠资本驱动增长变得愈发困难。这种突然的转变不仅导致融资更加困难，还促使公司开始专注于核心产品。正如你在这档播客中提到的，裁员、重组、管理层转向内部创业等现象频频出现。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Well, the one funny pocket was there's these large number of growth companies who have raised substantive dollars. So they're not going to run out of capital in 2022 or 2023. What's going to happen is, they actually have quite long periods of time, so you don't see them raising new rounds, you don't see them laying off, but in some ways they're still hiring or they're still seeking the next product. The sad truth is that many of their contemporary companies that went public are worth 10% or less than what they were worth back then, and these companies are privately held and so they're sort of sleeping in the shadows.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，许多已融资大量资金的增长型公司在2022年或2023年仍不存在资金短缺问题。问题在于，它们仍有很长一段时间的缓冲期——你看不到它们筹集新一轮融资，也看不到裁员，但某种程度上，它们仍在招聘新人或寻找下一个产品。令人痛心的是，许多已上市的同行公司的估值已跌至当时的十分之一，而这些私营公司则如同潜伏在阴影中的巨头。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: My fear is, from a career point of view, so many tech professionals are in these organizations or joining these organizations with the expectation that they'll make money on their equity, that they'll continue to do fine. And my sense is we're going to see, even in the second half of this year, lots of boards pulling back, taking their capital back, companies essentially saying, "Hey, we're capitalized. We're a scaled ocean liner, and now we need to go find product market fit." But doing that with 300 people and expectations of hitting a multi-billion dollar valuation just isn't going to happen. So that's the reason why I'm like, "Danger. This is not the company to join, this is the company to leave. Find another phase. Time's a wasting." And I worry very much that people aren't getting the message.
turns.zh: 从职业发展的角度来看，我担心许多科技从业者加入这类公司时，怀揣着通过股权获利、持续发展的期望。但我认为，即便在今年下半年，许多董事会也会收回资本，公司将不得不坦然承认：“嘿，我们已经获得了充足的资金。我们是一艘规模化的远洋轮船，现在需要重新寻找产品市场匹配点。”但要在300人团队中实现数十亿美元的估值，实在是痴人说梦。因此，我才会强调：“危险来临。这类公司不值得加入，而值得离开。寻找下一个发展阶段吧。时间紧迫了。” 我深切担忧人们没有领会到这个信号。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know you probably don't want to name any names of companies, but what are some signs that may be you're at one of these companies?
turns.zh: 我知道你可能不想点名具体公司，但能否列举一些可能身处这类公司的迹象？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I think that the moment that you are reframing the core product, trying to find that product market implies that this company's valuation needs to be a pre-product market fit valuation. So the two questions you ask yourself the day after we listen to this podcast is, "Hey, are we scaling a product? We have customers that love us and we have a tremendous sucking sound? Or are we trying to find that customer sucking sound?" And if the answer is, "We're still trying to find it," and then you're like, "Is your evaluation hundreds of millions or tens of millions?" and if the answer is hundreds or more and you're still trying to find that sucking sound, you're an ex-growth company.
turns.zh: 我认为，当你重新定义核心产品、试图寻找产品市场时，意味着这家公司的估值需要基于产品市场适配度进行评估。因此，在听完这期播客后的第二天，你需要问自己两个问题："嘿，我们是在扩展产品规模吗？我们已经有喜欢我们的客户，而且产品反响热烈？还是说我们仍在寻找客户需求？"如果答案是"我们仍在寻找客户需求"，那么你会想："你们的估值是数亿美元还是数千万美元？"如果估值达到数亿美元，而你仍在寻找客户需求，那你就是一家前景堪忧的成长型公司了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As a founder listening to this, I bet you're like, "Damn, we don't want people leaving. This isn't the kind of message we want to hear." On the other hand, as an employee at a company, that is your advice, just generally recognize it and then you should probably leave as soon as possible because things are not going to work out for you.
turns.zh: 作为听众的创业者，我敢打赌你会想："天啊，我们不想让员工离职。这可不是我们想听到的消息。"另一方面，作为公司员工，这就是你的忠告——你最好清醒认识到现实，然后尽快离开，因为事情对你的发展不利。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: As an employee, I think you have almost no recourse because you almost have to start over in terms of it's a new four-year investment. I think that as a founder, you can recap your company. You can reset your stock price, you could reissue. You can make those hard decisions and you can maybe return some of the money to the board and still continue, or you can pull the plug and restart the company that maybe you really wanted to. But I think the founder is in a better position, but they also have a lot more to lose and far more constraints. But employees, they're not... If you listen to this and come to this conclusion, a lot of times, the listeners here, half or more of their compensation is an equity and we just concluded that most of their equity may not be worth anything. In which case, are you willing to take a half pay cut or work for 20% of what you can get on the market? My question is, that seems to be quite concerning, the opportunity cost is just too rich.
turns.zh: 作为员工，我认为你几乎没有退路，因为这相当于要重新开始四年的投资。我认为作为创始人，你可以对公司进行重估。你可以重置股价，重新发行股票。你可以做出这些艰难决定，或许将部分资金返还董事会后继续前行，或许干脆停掉公司，重新启动你真正想做的事业。但创始人处境更优，但同时也面临更大风险和更多制约。至于员工，如果你听完播客得出这个结论，通常听众中半数以上的人薪酬以股权形式发放，而我们刚刚得出结论，他们的大部分股权可能一文不值。既然如此，你愿意接受减薪一半，或者接受市场上20%薪资水平的工作吗？我的问题是，这似乎相当令人担忧，机会成本实在太高了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: An important variable in this framework/piece of advice is product market fit. This might be too big of a question, but just, what tells you that something might have not have product market fit when you're at a company like this? What are signs to you and smoke signals of like, "They may not have product market fit"?
turns.zh: 在这个框架/建议中，产品市场适配度是一个重要变量。这或许是个过于宏大的问题，但请问，当你身处这样的公司时，如何判断产品可能缺乏产品市场适配度？哪些迹象和警示信号能让你意识到"他们可能缺乏产品市场适配度"？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: For me, it's always around this pull that sort of how much work do you have to do to basically generate pull? So right now with OpenAI for example, we're seeing ridiculous pull, but we may not be seeing, for example, massive revenue or profitability. So that's the reason why I tend to feel like you can kind of tell by how hard it is to acquire your users. When companies are putting very little in marketing and there're people coming into the door or there's such an easy sale, you've got it. I think that this sucking pull kind of concept feels like the most appropriate way to define it as opposed to the sort of unit economics of acquisition and time to pay back. There are lots of mathy ways to do it, but early on you can tell how hard are you working to bring people in the door.
turns.zh: 对我而言，关键在于产品的吸引力。比如OpenAI目前吸引力惊人，但我们可能尚未看到大量营收或盈利。因此，我倾向于通过获取用户的难度来判断。这家公司几乎不投放营销，但仍有客户主动上门，或销售过程异常顺畅，那就是成功的标志。我认为这种吸引力概念，比起获取用户的单位经济效益和回本周期，要更贴切地定义产品市场适配度。虽然有许多数学方法可以量化，但在早期阶段，你能明显感受到获取用户的难度。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there any reason to consider staying at a company like this?
turns.zh: 还有什么理由留在这样的公司吗？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: There are counter examples. I think the counterpoint is, this is the biggest role that you feel like you could get and you have an appetite to sort of learn like, "I'm on the executive team, I'm not going to get that somewhere else. That experience is career additive. I want that moment." Great. Sometimes I see loyalty come in, "This was my baby. I feel a commitment to the team, the team that I've made, et cetera."
turns.zh: 确实存在反例。我认为关键在于，这可能是你能获得的最重要的角色，你渴望学习——比如，“我身处高管团队，如果去别处就无法获得这种经验了。这种经历对职业生涯很有助益，我渴望把握住这个机会。” 好的。有时我能感受到员工的忠诚情结：“这是我的心血项目，我对团队负有责任，等等。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I actually respect that. I think that you have to put bounds on that. I think that you should have that conversation. But the learning position, the loyalty tend to be the primary reasons to maybe delay the decision, but fear of finding another job is a bad reason, but is an often common reason as well.
turns.zh: 我很尊重这种态度。我认为你需要为此设定界限，应该进行这样的对话。但学习型思维和忠诚感往往是延迟决策的主要原因，而恐惧找不到新工作却是个糟糕的借口，不过这种担忧确实很常见。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Now that we've given many listeners an existential crisis, let me move on to another question within the early career phase and then I'm going to move on to mid-career. I guess the question is just, is there any other piece of advice, wisdom for early PMs? Maybe the question is, what do you think they should most get right in their early career?
turns.zh: 既然我们已经让许多听众陷入了存在主义危机，让我们转向职业生涯早期阶段的另一个问题，然后再谈谈中期职业生涯。我想问的是，有没有其他建议或智慧之言给初级产品经理？或许问题在于，他们在职业生涯早期最应该做好什么？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: There's probably two answers that I would share. One is, they want to build something that they as much as possible are world-class in. So if you think about the different types of product ambiguities that exist in industry, you can be a great crafter. You could be incredibly strong at market ambiguity. You could understand how to navigate markets and create something new that doesn't exist. You can be great at organizational ambiguity. I know how to take complex teams that have complex goals and solve an inside the building problem. You can be a domain expert. I'm an ML expert, I'm a really strong hardware PM. You can be a team expert. I just really thrive in managing managers and I just know how to get the balance right. So, being a product manager means you're confronted with maybe all five or maybe more of these. I want to know that you pick up one of these as early as possible.
turns.zh: 可能有两个答案我想分享。第一，他们希望在尽可能多的领域做到世界级水准。举个例子，看看行业中存在的不同产品不确定性类型，你可以成为出色的产品设计师。你可能在市场不确定性方面极为强大。你能理解如何开拓新市场，创造出不存在的新产品。你可以擅长组织不确定性——我知道如何管理目标复杂、团队复杂的项目，解决内部问题。你可以成为领域专家——我是机器学习专家，或者是硬件产品经理。你可以成为团队专家——我善于管理管理者，只知道如何平衡各方关系。所以，成为产品经理意味着你可能要应对这五种甚至更多不确定性。我希望你尽早选择其中一种。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: So maybe you become an expert in domain, maybe you become a great crafter, maybe you really think through how to manage growth. Growth is another one that I would add to the list. But picking a lane is kind of goal number one. And then maybe goal number two is having a story to tell to that next employer and that next, next. What I worry about is, sometimes when I'm in an interview, and you and I have probably done hundreds, and you're talking to someone and then they talk about those early jobs and they just sort of said they were there, this happened and it's very hard to connect, tell me exactly what you learned and what you did, I want to know that story. So it's just like Amazon talks about building the press release before they start creating a product. Think about the story, think about the skill, then solve your day to day, your week to week, your month to month, your performance review. That's my biggest advice I seize.
turns.zh: 所以，或许你会成为某个领域的专家，或许你会成为出色的产品设计师，或许你会深入思考如何管理增长。增长也是我要补充的关键要素。但选择一条路线是首要目标。然后第二个目标是为下一份工作、再下一份工作准备好讲述自己的故事。我担心，面试时你和我们可能做过数百次面试，当你谈论早期工作经历时，他们只是说自己在那里待过，这事发生过，很难把学到的东西和实际行动联系起来。我希望听到你具体讲述了什么、做了什么。这就像亚马逊在开始开发产品前先构思新闻稿一样。先构思故事，再磨练技能，最后应对日常工作、每周任务和月度评估。这是我最珍视的建议。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that advice. It connects to your other earlier piece of advice, of just try to get a variety of experiences because that'll help you figure out which of these things is maybe best suited for what you're interested in, what you enjoy doing.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个建议。这与你早前的建议相呼应，即尽可能获取多样化经验，因为这能帮助你确定哪种不确定性最适合你的兴趣和喜好。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yep, absolutely.
turns.zh: 是啊，完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So let's transition to mid-career. Let's talk about promotions. You mentioned getting promoted earlier. We chatted a bit about that. There's probably no one ever that didn't want to get promoted. It's a common topic in people's career, but a lot of times people don't understand why they're not getting promoted, they're not sure people are looking for to get promoted. You've promoted a lot of people and you've gone through a lot of promotions. What would be your advice to give people who are trying to get promoted and just haven't been promoted? What would you suggest people in that position generally do?
turns.zh: 太棒了。那接下来我们转到职业生涯中期阶段。让我们聊聊晋升事宜。你之前提过自己晋升过一次，我们也稍微聊过这个话题。恐怕没有人不想获得晋升机会。这是职场中常见的话题，但很多人不明白为什么自己没能晋升，也不确定公司是否在寻找晋升人才。你晋升过很多人，经历过多次晋升过程。对于那些努力晋升却未能如愿的人，你有什么建议？对于处于这种境地的人，你通常会给出哪些建议？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah, it's a great question. I think that we want to kind of understand why, and oftentimes asking your manager won't reveal the answer. So then you'll start with that. I think that the answer of what you do is correlated with what's the real reason. And I think that there may be, I'll suggest four kind of common things I've seen that really hold people back. And then depending on your environment, you have to decide how many of these apply.
turns.zh: 嗯，这是个很棒的问题。我觉得我们需要先理解其中的原因，通常向上级询问并不能获得答案。所以首先你要从自身找原因。你的表现是否与真正的晋升标准相符？我认为可能存在四种常见的阻碍因素。具体情况因人而异，但你需要判断这些因素在你身上是否适用。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: So I think the number one is that you just don't have advocacy. You need someone to see the magic in you to be promoted. There is many of your listeners who have that magic but maybe have a manager or a promotion team, it doesn't always have to be the manager itself, who doesn't see said magic. And in that case, if you have the magic, you're in a bad setting and you just need to change. That could be a shift within the project. You could find a manager who sees it. It could be leaving the company. I think the second that's very common now, Lenny, and I think it's coming up a ton, is the next role doesn't exist.
turns.zh: 首先，可能是缺乏支持者。你需要有人看到你的闪光点，从而推动你的晋升。很多听众具备这些潜质，但他们的上级或晋升团队（不一定非得是直属上级）未能发现这些亮点。在这种情况下，如果你确实有能力，就说明所在环境不合适，你需要做出改变。比如换个项目组，找到认可你才能的上级，或者考虑离职等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: So this is not as present in hypergrowth because the next role always did exist. There was always growth, there was always hiring, you're always hiring people above you, below you, et cetera. Now, I think there's lots of examples of people who are really qualified and working at the next level, but the job doesn't exist. So you can't really create that job and ask them to be working at that next job if their position is mostly the previous one. Again, I feel like it's not that satisfying because it means you're still being held back, but it's radically different than if you're unqualified. These two are sort of more, the system is not in a position to advocate.
turns.zh: 在高速增长的公司，这种情况不常见，因为下一个晋升机会总是存在的。公司不断发展，持续招聘，职位层级分明，上下级结构清晰。但如今，许多资质出众的人晋升到下一个级别后，却发现职位空缺。这意味着你无法创造新职位并要求员工填补空缺，因为他们的现有职位与下一个级别职位存在重叠。这种情况比能力不足更令人沮丧，因为这意味着晋升受阻，但又与能力不足完全不同。归根结底，问题在于晋升体系缺乏支持机制。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: The third is when you are being impatient. And I think the hardest ones that I think I've worked with is, the highest performers have succeeded because they have set their goals to be more aggressive than what was essentially average achievable. By default, we expect you to be two years in this role. They're like, "Great, I'll see you in a year." And then they get frustrated when they can't do that, and leadership takes longer to absorb. It's more soft skills, it's more subtle. Oftentimes it's based on impact, which is a lot of times lagging, and that tends to be frustrating. So if listeners are like, "I know I'm used to being promoted annually and now I'm a leader and I'm not moving as quickly, it's time for me to go," I'm like, well, maybe that's working as intended. So impatience is a number three.
turns.zh: 第三个原因是缺乏耐心。比如那些最优秀的员工之所以能晋升，是因为他们设定的目标比平均可达目标更具挑战性。默认情况下，公司期望你能在某个职位上工作两年。但他们会说：“好吧，那我们一年后再见。”当他们无法达成目标时，又会感到沮丧，而领导层也需要更长时间来认可他们的表现。这更多是软技能方面的挑战，需要更细致的观察。通常这取决于影响力，而影响力往往滞后，这容易让人感到挫败。所以如果听众说：“我习惯每年晋升一次，现在我成了领导，却晋升速度变慢了，是时候离开了吧？”我会说，或许这正是正常的晋升机制在起作用。所以耐心不足是第三个原因。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: And then the fourth one I think is about 50% of the cases where it's really, there is a development area but it isn't quite connected to the individual. The listener has a development area, it's substantive. The manager is poor at identifying it, perhaps even doesn't see it, but the promotion committee does, the individual refuses to hear it, which is a very common one. Or they hear it and they just don't want to change it. And they don't do it because they're arrogant, they do it because it's like, "This is who I am. You want me to be X and I'm Y, and that's what a Y is and I don't want to be X." This is the hardest one because this is where coaching and development and self-awareness come in.
turns.zh: 接下来，我认为第四种情况占了约50%的比例，即存在发展空间，但与个人并未紧密结合。员工有发展潜力，而且这种潜力是实质性的。但管理者难以识别这一潜力，甚至可能视而不见，而晋升委员会却能察觉到。员工要么拒绝接受反馈（这种情况很常见），要么听取建议却不愿改变现状。他们之所以这样做，或许并非傲慢，而是出于自我认同——“我就是我，你想让我成为X，但我本质上是Y，我不想成为X。”这类情况最难处理，因为这正是辅导、发展和自我认知发挥作用的关键领域。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. This super resonates. So just to summarize the four reasons you may not be getting promoted: One is, there's no advocate that sees your magic and understands that you're awesome. Two is, there's no actual role that's available and so there's nothing to get promoted to. And that's so true right now, there's just not. Everyone's laying people off, they're getting rid of manager layers. I totally see that all over the place. Three is, you're probably just not being patient. Four, you actually have some work to do and you shouldn't be promoted. Maybe to follow a thread on that first one, if someone doesn't see your magic, I see a lot of people just complaining that like, "Oh, I'm doing so well, I'm so great and nobody understands it. No one gives me credit. No one really appreciates me." I don't know if there is an answer to this, but is there a way to help people see that no, you're actually not doing great versus you are and people just don't see it? What's a sign maybe? Maybe you're not as great as you think you might be.
turns.zh: 太棒了。这真的让我深有共鸣。总结一下，晋升受阻的四个原因：一是没有支持者能发现你的闪光点，认可你的价值。二是没有实际的晋升职位——晋升无从谈起。眼下确实如此，裁员潮汹涌，管理层架构精简，我到处都能看到这种现象。三是可能你缺乏耐心。四是你的确还有成长空间，不该晋升。或许回到第一个原因，如果别人看不到你的价值，我见过很多人抱怨：“我表现这么好，却得不到认可。” 我不知道有没有解决办法，但有没有办法让人们意识到，哦，实际上你表现并不出色，只是别人没看到呢？或许可以通过某种信号来传达？比如你可能并没有自己想象中那么优秀。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: The cheap answer is you have to get real feedback, not formal feedback. I think that the more scaled the company is, the more they have these systems in place which provide formal feedback. But honestly, we've run experiments where we said let's ignore the formal feedback, let's have a real conversation with my peers on how our teams are doing. The signal that comes out are dramatically different than the formal feedback. So what you're looking for when you feel like you're in this situation where you're not being seen, and it might be because there's a real issue, what you really want to dial into is, "Let me get the ground truth as to what people are thinking," and you have to have very strong listener skills where we all have been in the discussion, where you're giving feedback to someone and the next thing that they tell you is they justify how you're wrong, that you missed this. "Let me tell you about exactly why that situation that you're using wasn't..."
turns.zh: 简单粗暴的解决方案是获取真实反馈，而非形式化的评估。我认为公司规模越大，越倾向于建立正式反馈机制。但说实话，我们做过实验，故意忽略正式反馈，转而与同事深入探讨团队表现。得到的反馈与正式评估大相径庭。所以当你感觉自己未被认可，可能确实存在实际问题时，你真正需要做的是“深入了解人们的真实想法”，这需要强大的倾听能力。我们都经历过这样的场景：你给出反馈后，对方却反驳你的错误，说：“让我告诉你你用的那个案例根本不成立……”。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: You have to be great at pulling feedback, listening to it. You have to triangulate it from people that don't see you all the time, that do see you all the time, your peers. But you have to create an environment of safety where people feel like there is no worry about retaliation or concern, et cetera. And the more comfortable people are about giving feedback to you and the more you have the skills to pull it and you don't trust formal or you don't trust manager, the better shot you have of truly understanding what that real issue is and solving it.
turns.zh: 你必须善于收集反馈，倾听各方声音。需要从那些长期关注你的人、与你长期共事的人、同事等多角度获取信息。但你必须营造安全的环境，让人们无需担心遭到报复或评判。越是让人们乐于给你反馈，你越有能力收集这些反馈，同时越不信任正式反馈或管理层，你就越有可能真正理解问题所在并解决它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This reminds me of Jules Walter who's on the podcast. He gave a bunch of advice. I don't know if you saw that. I've had to accept feedback and get people to give you feedback. And one of its pieces of advice is, ask people for real feedback. And no matter how much you're melting inside hearing it, just be like, "Thank you so much for that." Because then, people feel like, "All right, he's listening."
turns.zh: 这让我想起了播客嘉宾朱尔斯·沃尔特（Jules Walter）。他给出过很多建议，不知道你是否听过。我必须学会接受反馈，并让别人为你提供反馈。其中一条建议是，真诚地请求别人给出真实反馈。无论听到反馈时内心多么不适，都要保持礼貌，说：“非常感谢你的反馈。”这样人们就会觉得，“好吧，他在认真倾听。”

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I think Jules is a great, probably one of the world's best people in pulling feedback in my experience. I think that the one that even ones up it is, when I talk to Jules, Jules will look for feedback, then he'll repeat it back to me better than even I presented it. And then I'd say, "Well, let me now feel safer to even provide." Because anyone who's explaining it to a place that they all not only internalize it but they can articulate clearly understands and values it. And that's the really powerful way is, "So what you're saying is I just interrupt far too often and some ways it's almost to a point that it's annoying. Is that a fair assessment?" "Oh, that's actually not the words I use," but that's what really gets people comfortable in sharing with you what's really going on.
turns.zh: 我认为朱尔斯在收集反馈方面堪称世界级高手，以我的经验来看，甚至超越了其他人。比如，我和朱尔斯交谈时，他会主动寻求反馈，然后比我更清晰地复述出来。这时我会说：“好吧，现在我更敢于坦诚分享了。”因为当别人不仅能内化你的观点，还能清晰表达并认可它的价值时，反馈才真正有效。例如，朱尔斯会说：“所以你的意思是，我经常打断别人，甚至到了让人厌烦的程度。这样评价公平吗？”对方可能会说：“哦，我不是这么说的。”但这种方式能让人们更自在地分享真实想法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I think we're discovering some of these people that have worked with you that have been on the podcast slowly. Maybe while we're on this topic, I didn't expect to go here, but in terms of other tips for getting good feedback, is there anything else that just comes top of mind of how to get better feedback from people? Because it's hard to do. Most people talk about getting feedback and then don't, or they just don't know how. So one is just, you said repeat back exactly what they told you and be like very appreciative. Is there anything else?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我觉得我们慢慢发现了许多曾参与播客的嘉宾。或许顺便说一下这个话题，虽然我没预料到会聊到这儿，但关于获取有效反馈的其他建议，你能想到最直接的方法是什么？因为这确实很难。大多数人嘴上说要收集反馈，却做不到，或者根本不知道怎么做。首先，你要准确复述对方的话，并表现出感激之情。还有别的办法吗？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I'd share out feedback. It's a little easier when you are a manager, but for example, most managers that are listening have a staff discussion. Maybe it's sort of awkward, but maybe you have a standup and you are giving notes to people. So as a manager, someone will come to me and they'll give me a piece of feedback. The next Monday when I have my staff meeting, I'll make a comment about something and I'll say, "Well, lot of this came because I got this great piece of feedback from..." and I'll name the person, and I'm like, "It really helped me see this challenge." Now, that feedback could be about me or about this project or about the team. And it might be positive, it might be constructive. People hear that and they're like, "Wow, I get recognized for giving this guy feedback. Sign me up." You're always trying to find way to break down that barrier.
turns.zh: 我会分享反馈。作为管理者会更容易些。比如，大多数倾听型管理者会组织员工讨论会。可能会有点尴尬，但你也可以在站立会议上给出反馈。作为管理者，当有人来找我反馈时，我会在下周一的员工会议上提及此事：“很多启发都来自于我收到的一份很棒的反馈……”，然后点名具体人员，并说：“这真的帮助我看清了挑战所在。” 反馈可能针对我个人、项目或团队。可能是正面的，也可能是建设性的。人们听后会感叹：“哇，给我反馈的人居然被认可了。算我一个。” 你总要想办法打破障碍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that tip. You talked about managers and how often managers are not great at managers. Maybe they don't identify development areas, maybe they're bad in other areas. So maybe just a question here of just, why are managers often not great? And then two, if you're a new manager, I think a lot of listeners are maybe transitioning to management or about to transition, what's your advice for being successful as a new manager?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个建议。你提到管理者往往不善于管理，或许他们不善于识别员工发展空间，或在其他方面做得不好。那么，第一个问题，管理者为什么常常做得不好？第二个问题，如果你是新晋管理者（很多听众可能正在向管理层过渡或即将过渡），你有什么建议能助其成功？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I'll start by saying that, in a hundred years when the archeologists look back and they see tech in the sort of early years of tech, the first 34 years, they'll say that the biggest surprise was how much we thought it was okay to not train managers. The military probably didn't make that mistake for very long before they corrected it. And most immature industries really train managers, but boy, if you're a good coder, you are ready to manage. That's the way the industry works. If you can talk, you are ready to product manage. If you can product manage and ship something out the door, you should definitely tell people what to do. I think that there's such a loose coupling between the skills to be successful at building things and teaching people how to build. It's the difference between if you can make a good car, you must know how to make the factory that makes the car. I don't think that's true at all.
turns.zh: 先说一句，百年后当考古学家回顾科技史，尤其是早期34年的科技发展时，他们最大的惊讶或许在于，我们竟曾认为不培训管理者是合理的。军方在这方面犯过错，但很快就纠正了错误。而大多数新兴行业确实会培训管理者，但说真的，如果你是个优秀的程序员，就足以胜任管理工作。这个行业就是这样运作的——如果你能说话，就能做产品经理；如果你能做产品经理并成功交付项目，那你肯定能指挥团队。我认为，在成功构建产品与教导他人构建产品之间，存在着严重的技能脱节。就像造好一辆车，就必须懂如何建造汽车工厂。这根本不成立。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I think that this is a massive epidemic, that I think there's the thousand challenges that stem from this, whether it's challenges around bias, challenges around enabling coaching and teaching and solving development areas. My hope is that one day as an industry we find ways to improve and fix it. But podcasts like yours are actually quite meaningful steps. I would say that your podcast might be more meaningful than most L&D departments in most organizations today. So that's powerful because you're having a tremendous amount of impact, and I think learning is essentially a lifelong opportunity and I think that is the type of resources that just didn't exist a decade ago.
turns.zh: 我认为这是一个严重的行业顽疾，由此衍生出千种挑战——无论是偏见问题，还是如何赋能指导与教学，乃至解决开发难题。我期待这个行业终有一天能找到改进之道。但像您这样的播客，无疑是意义深远的举措。我敢说，在当今多数组织中，您的播客比绝大多数学习与发展部门都更有价值。这意义非凡，因为您正产生着巨大影响力。我深信学习本应是终身机遇，而这类资源资源十年前根本不存在。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I think to answer your question around what are the common pitfalls, if you're a first time manager listening or maybe someone who's considering it, I think there are probably two quick things that I would say you have to get bravely thoughtful about as you enter into this journey. One is, your challenge is going to be to share the steering wheel with the person or the set of people you are managing. And I think that there's this three modes that people have in their head. They're like, "Oh, management is divide and conquering. You go there, I go there, we meet up."
turns.zh: 谈到新手管理者常犯的误区，如果您正初次担任管理者或正考虑转岗，我认为有两点需要勇敢反思。首先，您必须学会与团队成员共同掌控方向盘。这里有三种思维模式：第一种是“分而治之”——各自为战，最后汇总结果；第二种是“传授骑行技巧”——先手把手教，再放手让学员独立；第三种则类似摩托车副驾驶——驾驶者负责主控，副驾驶负责提供指导。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Or they'll say it's like riding a bike, or teaching to ride a bike, I should say. Someone starts out on the bicycle, I hold your hand, I let go, and then I hope that you fly. I think it's more like the sidecar on the motorcycle, where person's driving the motorcycle and I'm on the sidecar and whether I like it or not, I'm attached, but I have this relatively specific role of giving counsel. I think that that model of how do you share the steering wheel, not just say you got it or I got it or I got it for a while, and then I hand it to you is the key question.
turns.zh: 我更倾向于后者：副驾驶虽受驾驶者约束，但必须担负具体的指导职责。关键在于如何合理分配控制权，而不是简单地“我来”或“你来”，然后再交还控制权。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: And then I think that the second miss that people tend to have is they tend to, because they have power, by the way, organizational power, not because they've earned that power, they start managing whatever they define that to be. And what I find is that you're more like the vampire knocking on the door of someone. You have to be invited in. You just can't walk through the threshold. And I think that no matter how senior the person that is the manager, you have to earn the right to be the person's manager. So maybe to be specific, well, if I start managing someone, the thing I'd like to understand is like, "Hey, well, what can I help you with?" And they can invite me in. Oftentimes, the answer is, "I don't need you. I actually wasn't excited about you as a manager. I don't need another layer between you and the CEO. Get out." And I'm like, "That's cool," because anything I say after that is just going to be annoying and it's going to backfire.
turns.zh: 接下来，我认为人们常犯的第二个误区是，他们往往因为拥有权力——尤其是组织层面的权力（而非靠自身努力获得的权力）——就开始管理自己定义的任何事务。但我发现，你更像是敲别人家门的吸血鬼。你必须被邀请进来，不能强行闯入。无论管理者职位多高，你都必须赢得管理他人的资格。比如，我要开始管理某个人时，首先会问：“嘿，你需要我帮什么忙？”对方可能会回应：“我不需要你。我对你的管理能力本来就不感兴趣。我不需要你在CEO和员工之间再加一层。出去吧。”我通常会说：“好吧”，因为接下来的话都会显得惹人生气，只会适得其反。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Now, one day they will need help, and I will be in the sidecar waiting to say, "Perhaps I can assist." And then when you finally get to that moment where you're invited in, you pick an area or two, and then you really partner with that person on that area. I can give examples on that, but I generally think that it's this invitation picking specific and then making sure we're sharing the responsibility is the key set of notes that I would share with you.
turns.zh: 总有一天，他们会需要帮助，而我会坐在副驾驶座上等着说：“或许我能帮上忙。”当你终于获得被邀请的机会时，你可以选择一两个领域，然后与对方在这些领域展开深度合作。我可以举例说明，但我认为关键在于获得邀请、明确具体职责并确保责任共担，这才是我要分享给你们的核心要点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's your take on the IC path, senior IC path, something that a lot of companies talk about? I know Meta is big on this right now, the layering managers and things like that. I find a lot of times there's a lot of talk about it and there's not really a real career opportunity there. I guess, what's your just take on as that is a real option for most people trying to basically avoid the manager out and staying in IC, PM long term?
turns.zh: 你对IC路径（尤其是高级IC路径）有什么看法？很多公司都在谈论这个话题，我知道Meta现在特别重视这点，比如分层管理之类的。但我发现很多时候大家只是空谈，却没有真正的职业发展机会。我想问问你，对大多数试图避免成为管理者、长期停留在IC或PM岗位的人来说，这是否真的是一个可行的选择？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah, I think that it's a little bit more acute now because of the backlash that we talked about between growth where management was perceived. So in this case, management was perceived as a way to drive expansion. So if you're in charge of expansion, you're managing the people that are doing the build and now we're doing a lot fewer things. So I think that's what's mandated this sort of growth in the IC track, for lack of a better term. I think it is one of the best things that happened to our industry because what's happened is, in the last 10 years, and you can tell I'm particularly hard on our managers here, they've basically been promising ICs that early promoted into management. They didn't get taught, and now they're sort of average managers and promising ICs. But now the story that they tell and what they've built is not awesome.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为现在这个问题更加尖锐，因为我们之前提到的增长型思维模式让管理被视为推动扩张的手段。所以如果你负责扩张，就会管理那些负责构建的人员，而现在这类工作已经大幅减少。因此，我认为这推动了IC路径的增长（找不到更合适的词汇了）。我认为这是我们行业最积极的变化之一，因为过去10年间——你能看出来我对我们的管理者特别不满——他们基本上承诺早期晋升管理层的IC们，他们没有得到系统的培训，现在成了普通的管理者和失意的IC。但他们讲述的故事和创造的成果并不令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: If I'm looking to hire, if I'm in a growth company and I'm the next hottest thing and I'm looking to hire someone and someone walks into the interview and said, "Look, I've managed two people before and then I was in the charge of this thing, but they really did the details. And then by the way before that, I was early in trying to get this thing out the door and then they picked me to be manager," I'm like, "Okay, that's an interesting set of experiences. I'm looking, for me, in my company to build something."
turns.zh: 如果我要招聘员工，如果我在一家热门公司，刚崭露头角，准备招聘某个人，而这个人走进面试间说：“看，我之前管理过两个人，然后负责过这个项目，但都是他们具体操作的。而在那之前，我早期负责把这个项目推向市场，然后他们选我当了经理。”我会说：“好吧，这是一段有趣的经历。但我现在在公司是想打造些东西。”

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: The next person walks in, it's like, "I've been an IC for that whole time. And during that time I went from learning something to demonstrating it to really being able to take it forward. And I got one of these ambiguities master. I'm an expert in domain. I'm an expert in managing organizations," I'm like, "I don't need a team ambiguous expert. That's not my hard part. My hard part is actually cracking the code on this complex market or this very complicated organization where we have two teams that have different goals. You're the type of person I want."
turns.zh: 下一个人走进来时，他会说：“我一直担任IC（Individual Contributor）角色。在这段时间里，我从学习到展示，再到真正能推动项目进展。我还获得了‘歧义处理大师’认证。我是领域专家，也是组织管理专家。”我会说：“我不需要一个‘团队歧义处理专家’。这不是我最难的地方。对我来说，真正的挑战是破解复杂市场或组织难题，比如当两个团队目标不一致时该如何应对。你才是我需要的人才。”

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: So I think Lenny, to your question, I think the IC track is one of the best things that's going to happen for people career. But to your point, those tracks, from a promotion and from a industry, how we perceive it, they're not in cement yet. They're tender. You wait six months, you wait nine months, they'll become very, very strong and solid. And I think then, we'll be able to lean very hard into them as a real promising crack for builders.
turns.zh: 所以我认为莱尼，针对你的问题，我认为IC（Individual Contributor）路径是职业生涯中最有前景的机遇之一。但从晋升和行业角度来看，这些路径目前还不够完善。它们还处于成长期，需要时间沉淀。等六个月、九个月后，它们会变得更加成熟和稳固。到那时，我们就能真正将其作为建设者的重要机遇大力推进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Your sense is, this is going to become more and more real as these layoffs have happened and kind of pullbacks on growth have happened.
turns.zh: 你的观察很到位，随着裁员和增长放缓的现实情况出现，这些问题将愈发凸显。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, if you think about it, it's the reality in engineering and design. So in engineering, you can be the sort of VP of engineering or CTO, and in a design, a lot of designers become design managers, a lot of them stay as crafters. And then for whatever reason in product managers, maybe because they were managers in our title, we just all became managers. What about the product? What about the other side? So I actually think it's a bug that has existed for a long time that actually we're going to correct permanently now.
turns.zh: 是的，我的意思是，这在工程和设计领域都是常态。在工程领域，你可以成为工程副总裁或首席技术官；在设计领域，许多设计师会成为设计经理，更多人继续担任创意工作者。然而在产品经理领域，可能是由于我们原有的职位头衔，我们都被简单地归为管理者。那产品方面呢？其他角色呢？所以我认为这是一个长期存在的缺陷，现在我们终于要彻底纠正它了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I wonder if part of it for PMs is, once you become a manager, this happens to me, I didn't want to be an IC anymore. It's like, "I'm done with that. I really enjoy this management layer." And I imagine with engineers, maybe they'll enjoy the coding. When I was an engineer I was like, "Oh, I don't want to just sit around and manage. I just want to code." So I wonder if there's any part of that.
turns.zh: 我想知道产品经理是否也存在这样的情况。一旦成为管理者（我也经历过），产品经理就不再想做IC了。他们会说：“我受够了。我真的很享受管理层的工作。” 而工程师可能更喜欢编码。当我还是工程师时，我会说：“哦，我不想只是坐着管理，我只想编码。” 所以我想这其中可能有一些共通之处。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: But a lot of your listeners like to build. And actually, when they talk to their managers, they're like, "I don't know if that job is awesome. It feels like you spend all your time writing docs and telling your boss's boss what to justify resources and headcount. I just want to build stuff. You don't build stuff." So I think there might be some of that. I think that it's not perfect, but I think hopefully builder and IC will become more synonymous.
turns.zh: 但很多听众都喜欢动手开发。实际上，当他们与经理沟通时，会说：“我不确定这个职位是否很棒。感觉你所有时间都在写文档，向老板的老板解释如何申请资源和招聘人数。我只想开发产品。但你根本不让我开发产品。” 所以我认为可能存在这样的问题。虽然目前还不完美，但希望产品开发者和IC（Individual Contributor）能更加互通有无。

turns.en: This episode is brought to you by Eppo. Eppo is a next generation A/B testing platform built by Airbnb alums for modern growth teams. Companies like DraftKings, Zapier, ClickUp, Twitch, and Cameo rely on Eppo to power their experiments.
