turns.zh: 曾在Airbnb工作时，我最喜欢的一点是公司的实验平台——我能按设备类型、国家、用户阶段等维度切分数据。Eppo能实现这些功能，甚至更胜一筹：它能快速产出分析结果，避免陷入冗长的分析循环，还能助你轻松锁定发现的任何问题的根源。Eppo支持前端与后端测试、邮件营销，甚至机器学习场景。欢迎访问geteppo.com了解详情。没错，就是geteppo.com。让实验速度提升十倍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coming back to the manager life and how many managers are not great and also just how do you get better as a manager, what have you found actually is effective in helping new managers become better?
turns.zh: 回到管理者角色的话题，许多管理者表现不佳，而你又该如何提升管理能力呢？你发现了哪些有效的方法能帮助新晋管理者成长？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I think I may have come across kind of hard on managers and I think I kind of said, "Hey, your manager and your manager's manager isn't really doing much teaching. Find the right podcast, good luck." And I think that that's a pretty soulless answer. So maybe the way I describe it is, well, I think learning is changing, and there's the self-service tools that are getting better and then there's the structured teaching which I think is weak. And then there's community, which I think whether it's within your company or outside of company, I think is the answer that we'll see more and more. I think community as a way of creating safety, having authentic conversations, feeling that you're not alone, that others are going through the same thing, and then sharing best practices is so powerful. And what social software has done is it has really empowered community.
turns.zh: 我觉得自己对管理者可能有些苛刻，曾说过“你的直属上司和上上司根本不怎么提供指导。去找个合适的播客看看吧，祝你好运。” 现在看来这确实是个冷酷的回答。或许我该这样描述：学习方式正在变革。自助式工具在不断优化，但结构化教学却存在缺失。而社区，无论是公司内部还是外部，必将成为更主流的学习平台。社区能创造安全感，让人们坦诚交流，感受到不孤单，知道其他人也在经历相似的挑战，还能分享最佳实践。社交软件为社区赋能的效果尤为显著。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: And now the tools are awesome. How many great communities have Slack channels or Discord channels or Zoom calls? And we do a lot of that in the CPO community that I created. Whether you're a new manager or whether you belong to a diverse group, whether you are new to a company, I think that all of your listeners should be part of an active community where they can be very authentic and very safe. Sometimes it's hard to do that with your coworkers, and so you need to find another community. Unfortunately, those communities are not the easiest to find today, but I believe that the notion of community as a powerful propellant for learning is the critical ingredient and hopefully many people are creating these communities so that new managers can find the right services.
turns.zh: 如今的工具太棒了。Slack频道、Discord群组、Zoom会议中诞生了多少优秀的社区？我在创建的CPO社区中也积极实践这些方式。无论你是新晋管理者，还是身处多元团队，或是初入新公司，我都建议听众加入活跃的社区。在那里你能保持真诚，获得安全感。有时与同事交流太难，这时就需要寻找其他社区。遗憾的是，现在这类社区不易寻觅，但我相信社区作为学习的强大助推器，将成为关键要素。希望更多人能创建这样的社区，让新晋管理者能找到合适的资源。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you actually talk about this community that you've built? This could be a good time to talk about it. It's called The Skip. Is that right?
turns.zh: 能具体谈谈你创建的社区吗？现在正是个好机会。它叫The Skip，对吗？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah. It's funny, it's all kind of fun products. They were always a reaction to something. They weren't really intentional. I, as you opened the podcast, did really enjoy teaching and coaching. I learned just as much from coaching others as they learned, I think. And yet I couldn't really scale. So I had this summer where I had just come off of being a head of product, and more and more of my people I was talking to were also head of products. What would happen is, I would have these conversations and they would ask me a question. I would say, "Well, that's the same conversation I answered on Tuesday." What you realize is, it's a very lonely job. Being lonely at the top is not just an adage. Really, everyone's so busy now. It's like, how do you have time to connect? Everything's a single player, you don't really have community.
turns.zh: 是啊。这挺有趣的，都是些好玩的产品。它们往往都是对某种情况的回应，并非刻意为之。正如我在开播时所说，我确实很喜欢教学和指导他人。我觉得自己从指导他人中收获的知识，跟他们从我这里学到的一样多。然而，我始终没能实现规模化发展。那年夏天，我刚卸任产品负责人，身边越来越多的人也都身处同样的职位。当我与他们交流时，他们会问我同样的问题。我会回答：“这问题我周二刚回答过。”你会意识到，这份工作实在太孤独了。“高处不胜寒”可不只是句俗语。如今每个人都太忙碌了，要如何找到时间交流呢？一切都是单打独斗，根本没有社交圈子。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: So I thought, "Well, what if I took the half a dozen people I talked to this month?" And I just said, "Hey, all of you are all interested in talking through how to navigate this crazy world of year one, year two, chief product officer. I think you would really gain. I know all of you and I think you can be safe with one another. Why don't we spend some time together?" So we did a WhatsApp channel and we brought a Zoom call. This was during the pandemic, so you really couldn't meet up. And we started talking. We started talking every month, and people were so empowered by the fact that the problem they were hitting was not just them. It was, "My crazy CEO is telling me this." And the next person is like, "Oh yeah? Let me tell you what my person said." And then they would say, "Oh my gosh, that sounds worse than my situation."
turns.zh: 于是我想到：“那何不把这个月交流过的六个人召集起来？”我说：“嘿，你们都对如何应对第一年、第二年、首席产品官等阶段的挑战感兴趣。我觉得你们会收获颇丰。我了解你们所有人，相信你们能互帮互助。何不一起共度时光？”我们创建了WhatsApp群组，还定期组织Zoom会议。当时正值疫情期间，大家难得见面。我们每月相聚，人们发现自己遇到的问题并非个例，而是普遍存在的——“疯狂的CEO总对我指手画脚”，“我也遇到过这种情况”，“天啊，你的状况比我的还要糟糕”……

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: But then, we would sit down and say, "Hey, the third person said I actually kind of had this and now I figured out a way out, and here's what I did." And you're like, "Wow, that's amazing. I'm going to try it." The next day they come back, they're like, "It works." And we started to connect and we built this trust, and community building is interesting and powerful work. So six went to 12, and then 12 went to 15, and now we have 28 members. A lot of folks are interested in these types of communities, but I'm so worried about scaling it because it's the enemy of trust and authenticity. So for all of you that are building communities, it's like tree balancing act. But I do think that the goal is to find ways to take all of this sort of like-minded folks that are in these same situations and connect them together. Late stage chief product officer happened to be one of the ones that had some of the most substantial importance to me because of all the coaching I did for that group.
turns.zh: 但随后我们会坐下来，听第三个人说：“我也遇到过这种情况，现在找到解决办法了，方法如下。”你会惊叹：“哇，太棒了！我要试试看。”第二天他们反馈：“确实有效。”我们逐渐建立信任，社群建设既有趣又有力。最初的六人组后来发展到12人，再到15人，如今已有28名成员。许多人对这类社群感兴趣，但我特别担心规模化扩张会损害信任和真实性。对于所有社群建设者而言，这就像在树上保持平衡的游戏。但我坚信目标在于将处境相似、志同道合的人们连接在一起。晚期阶段的首席产品官群体对我意义非凡，因为我为他们提供了大量指导。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If someone's listening and they're like, "Oh, I need to join this thing," how do they find out about it? How do they potentially apply and try to join?
turns.zh: 如果有人听完后想加入，该如何了解相关信息？又该如何申请加入？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Well, we have enough members now. There's a LinkedIn area called The Skip CPO Community, and you should contact any of the members that you know and ask them to join. My request and my requirement is that they are, number one, product leaders in their organization and a company that's not early, but that's mid to late. And the reason being is, those sets of problems tend to be the most similar. To be honest, I think this is not the only community that I want to be part of and help create, but this one happens to be the preexisting one. I think there are lots of powerful communities that can be created, but this particular one is very much focused on The Skip CPOs.
turns.zh: 嗯，我们现在已经有足够的成员了。领英上有个叫“Skip CPO社区”的专区，你应该联系你认识的成员，邀请他们加入。我的要求和期望是，他们首先要是在各自公司担任产品负责人，且所在公司不处于初创阶段，而是处于中期或后期阶段。原因在于，这些类型的公司面临的问题往往最为相似。说实话，我想参与和助力创建的社区不止这个，但这个恰好是现成存在的。我认为可以创建许多强大的社区，但这个社区特别专注于产品负责人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I'll mention the community around my newsletter just so folks are looking for a community join. I try not to promote these sorts of things, but it's a good time, may as well. If you're a paid subscriber to my newsletter, there's a Slack community you get access to. There's about 12, 13,000 people in there. There's meetups happening all over the world every month. It's amazing. Very proud of it. People are getting a lot of value of it, and it's basically open to any level of product manager. Other functions are in there too. So it's a very different sort of experience, but willing to add that also in the show notes if you want to check that.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我会在我的新闻通讯里提一下这个社区，这样大家就能知道要加入哪个社区了。我尽量不推广这类东西，但现在正好可以借机宣传一下。如果你是我的付费订阅用户，你可以加入一个Slack社区，里面有大约12、13000人。每个月全球各地都会举办聚会。真是太棒了。我为此感到非常自豪。大家从中获得了巨大的价值，而且这个社区基本面向所有级别的产品经理。其他职能部门的人也在里面。所以这是一种截然不同的体验，但如果你有兴趣，我愿意把相关信息加到节目笔记里。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I think that that would be my put, because so many of the managers will say, "Hey, I'm an IC," here's a greater one, "I am not being told I have the next job. I just was told to become an IC and I was a manager. I feel like my learning opportunities are stuck, but this is a bad time to look for a job." They should be in your community. They will learn more from that community than they will learn from managing one random person that they were attached to managing in some project that may or may not see the light of day, yet that's how our society is programmed. Our industry is like, "No, no, go manage that person because that's going to make you closer to the top. Forget learning." And I'm like, "Well, learning isn't happening. Learning's happening in your community. Learning is happening in our communities in general." That's why I'm pushing so hard on this.
turns.zh: 我觉得这就是我的观点，因为很多管理者会说：“嘿，我是个IC（独立贡献者）。”或者更严重一点：“我没有被告知下一个职位是什么。只是被告知要成为IC，而我之前是个经理。我觉得自己的学习机会被卡住了，但现在找工作又不是个好时机。”他们应该加入你的社区。他们能从这个社区学到比管理某个项目中随机分配给他们的人更多的东西，而这些项目可能最终未能成型，但我们的社会就是这样设定的。我们的行业会说：“不，不，赶紧去管理那个人，这样你才能更接近高层。别管学习了。” 而我要说：“嗯，学习根本没发生。学习是在你的社区里发生的。总的来说，学习是在我们的社区里发生的。” 这就是我为什么如此大力推动这个项目的原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is a good segue to talking about the third bucket, which is kind of later career CPOs. That's the segue in my mind there. Something that I've heard you talk about is that a lot of really senior leaders have real development areas, but they're hiding behind these superpowers that they have. Plus, people don't like to give real feedback to senior people. So I'd love to hear just what you're seeing there and how maybe people can work through that and what we can learn about that issue that you've noticed.
turns.zh: 这正好可以过渡到第三个话题——职业生涯后期的CPO们。这就是我脑海中的过渡点。据我所知，许多资深领导者都有实际的成长空间，但他们却隐藏在自己的超强能力背后。此外，人们也不愿意给高层人员提供真实反馈。所以我很想听听你对此的看法，以及大家如何克服这些问题，或者我们能从你观察到的这些问题中学到什么。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: This came from my notes as I was talking to a therapist on this. They talked about the shadows of superpowers. And I thought it was an incredibly powerful phrase that everyone focuses on your superpowers, but no one ever thinks about what shadows they create. Shadows of superpowers to me is the story of a lot of executives. There's an adage that's thrown around, which is, what gets you there isn't what got you here. It's sort of the tools that have made you successful today, you need to almost rebuild or relearn to get to the next phase. And I think both of these sort of speak to the same point, that oftentimes people have a great superpower. They go into a performance review, person says, "You're getting some feedback from your peers that you struggle in collaboration." And the manager even sometimes is puzzled, but the individual will say, "Are you kidding me? My last five performance reviews told me that I was one of the best collaborators in the company. How in the world is that possible?"
turns.zh: 这段文字源自我与一位心理治疗师探讨此话题时的笔记。他们谈及超级能力的阴影。我认为这是一个极具洞察力的表述——当所有人都聚焦于你的超能力时，却无人关注其背后所产生的阴影。超级能力的阴影，于我而言，是许多高管的写照。有一句广为流传的谚语：带你成功的并非曾助你成功的因素。那些助你登上巅峰的工具，在迈向新阶段时往往需要彻底重构或重新学习。这两句话都指向同一个核心问题——人们往往拥有某项卓越的超能力。当绩效评估时，上司会说：“同事反馈你协作能力不足。”被评估者甚至会困惑地说：“开玩笑吧？过去五次绩效评估都说我是公司最善于协作的人之一。这怎么可能？”

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: And then what you realize is that, "Well, you're collaborating as long as people agreed with your point of view. Now as a leader, we're asking you to be opinionated, and because you just think you're an amazing collaborator using the exact same tool set. And it turns out that when you're dealing with senior people, that may not even be in your function, they may not be product, they may not be tech, they recoil, but you're moving so fast because it's your superpower. You would never think that this needs to be rebuilt." Sometimes it could be more extreme. Great collaborators sometimes are very reticent to present their own opinions because they're so good at assimilating others. Or people that are amazing at growth struggle to be innovative. People that are world-class storytellers struggle to get in the details. People that are very taste maker, they are always the first to have point of view. They don't necessarily introduce change particularly often. You're strong politically, but your decisions are unprincipled. You're a structured thinker, but blue-sky innovations are very tough. You're an amazing listener, but you're very weak to be decisive. I can go on forever.
turns.zh: 此刻你会意识到：“好吧，你之所以善于协作，是因为大家都认同你的观点。如今作为领导者，我们要求你要有主见感，但你仍在用同样的工具包自视为顶级协作者。结果当你面对资深高管——无论是不同部门的同事、产品团队还是技术团队——他们都退避三舍，因为你的超能力太强了。你从未意识到这些需要重建。”

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: And what I would say to you is, sometimes even in a 30-minute conversation, walking into the room, just knowing what I know about the person, I can unlock their development area faster than anyone ever before, simply because my secret is, I'll bet you, because of this person's world-class here, these are the three things they're going to hit. And they don't even realize it because it's their identity. This is what got me here. If you make me work on that, you will make me change my superpower. And I'm like, "That's why you're stuck. That's why your career is plateauing." And then they get sad and then they take a long time to process, and then the work actually begins and then they solve and they go. Almost everyone, once they have the name and the face, they're able to solve. But facing the name is hard when it's sitting in the shadows of superpowers.
turns.zh: 我想对你们说的是，有时即便在30分钟的对谈中，只要了解对方的过往，我就能比以往任何人都更快地锁定他们的发展方向，原因很简单——我的秘诀是，我敢打赌，基于此人世界级的某项专长，他们必将遭遇以下三个挑战。但他们从未意识到，因为这已深深融入他们的身份。这就是他们成功的根源。若强迫他们改进超能力，就是要他们舍弃自我。我会说：“这就是你停滞不前的原因。这就是你的职业生涯触顶的原因。”他们会难过很久，迟迟无法接受现实，直到真正开始行动并解决问题后才释怀。几乎所有人一旦了解了问题的本质，都能找到解决之道。但当问题隐藏在超级能力的阴影中时，直面它就变得异常困难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. That is an incredibly important point. For someone to recognize this, do you find that they need someone like you that's like a coach, mentor, person to come in, and be like, "Here's what I see"? Or is there a way, I guess, as someone that's a peer or an employee to help them recognize this without them shutting down and being like, "No, shut up. No problem'?
turns.zh: 哇。这真是个极其重要的观点。你觉得要让别人意识到这一点，他们需要像你这样的人来充当教练、导师，或者直接告诉他们：“这是我看到的问题所在。”还是说，有没有其他办法，比如让同行或下属帮助他们认识到这一点，而不让他们感到抵触，说：“不，闭嘴。没问题的！”

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: No, you don't need a coach. What you do need is to listen to contradictory feedback. So what was the premise here is you're being told that something that you hold as your strength is actually in your way or a development area. Do not dismiss that. Recognize most likely you're doing it correctly. You just have gotten to the next level. So what I'm hoping the listener does is it goes back through all the feedback that they may even have and then looks at all the discard stuff. What's on the discard pile? Things that were discarded are anomalies because they're artifacts of my strength. And often, your managers are the ones that do the discarding, "Oh, that was just a weird... That person, they were just into it. They have it out for you. They got reorged or they were upset." I'm like, "No, no, no, no, no, no, no, no. Perception's reality. Talk to me about that one. That might be it." That's what I'm looking for.
turns.zh: 不，他们不需要教练。他们需要的是倾听相矛盾的反馈。所以这里的核心观点是，当被告知你自认为的强项实际上成了阻碍或发展瓶颈时，不要忽视这些反馈。很可能你做得没错，只是到了新的阶段。所以我希望听众能回顾所有可能收到的反馈，然后审视那些被忽视的部分。那些被搁置的反馈是什么？被搁置的意见往往是异常值，因为它们是你的强项的副产品。很多时候，给你反馈的人会说：“哦，那只是个奇怪的想法……那个人就是对你的成见。他们就是针对你的。他们被重组了，或者心情不好。” 我会说：“不，不，不，不，不，不，不不。认知即现实。跟我谈谈这个问题。可能就是这个原因。” 这才是我所关注的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fascinating. This makes me think about companies that have the same issue, companies strengths, like say Meta for example, move fast and break things and then, "Oh, that ends up being the biggest Achilles' heel." Uber, similar. Airbnb has similar challenges like that.
turns.zh: 太有意思了。这让我想到那些存在同样问题的公司，比如Meta，快速行动、突破现状，结果却发现这是最大的弱点；Uber也是如此；Airbnb也有类似的挑战。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Absolutely. This exact thing applies to relationships. This applies to companies, this applies to a lot. And I'm so happy that I was able to learn about it. Frankly, it was a critical unlock for me because I was stuck on something for years and I just could not understand how, for me, it was, I was very opinionated about something. And then I realized being loosely held on my opinions didn't mean that I became a weaker executive, but it was my opinions that got me to be so successful and it required me to rewire who I was as an executive. And that took a lot of time and a lot of energy. But it came from this realization and then I started to apply it for other strength areas. And now, every time I have a strength area of myself for those that I coach, I immediately talk through all the things that I bet you exist and most of the time were right.
turns.zh: 确实如此。这同样适用于人际关系、公司管理等诸多领域。我很高兴能从中领悟到这一点。坦白说，这对我来说是一个关键的突破。我曾多年深陷某个问题，却始终不明白为什么。我对某件事固执己见。但后来我意识到，灵活看待自己的观点并不意味着成为更弱的领导者，而是这些观点成就了我的成功。这需要我重塑作为领导者的自我认知。这花费了大量时间和精力。但正是从这个认知出发，我开始将其应用于其他强项领域。现在，每当我为所指导的人识别他们的强项时，我总会首先梳理那些你肯定存在、且大多正确的认知。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what is it for you that you said was your superpower and your shadow?
turns.zh: 那么，你所说的超级能力和盲点是什么？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I think that I was, as an entrepreneur, very opinionated about using small amounts of information to make decisions. And then I was very good at driving those things. So when you become an entrepreneur, you're great at grit, you're great at opinion, you're great at being decisive. And then as an executive, you spend a lot of time making sure everyone has context, everyone is heard, your opinions are actually edited for good reason. And it's not just to placate, it's actually to improve. But as someone who's basically been right a lot, that requires almost a complete and you're like, "Well, that's not who I am." And I'm like, "Okay, you start with the sentence like that's not who I am." You're definitely doing it right when you hit your leadership.
turns.zh: 我认为作为创业者，我对利用少量信息做决策非常固执己见。然后我很善于推动这些决策。成为创业者后，你擅长坚持、善于表达意见、善于果断决策。而作为高管，你需要花大量时间确保每个人都能理解背景、被倾听，你的意见经过合理编辑，不只是为了安抚他人，而是为了改进。但作为一个长期正确的人，这需要近乎彻底的转变。你会说：“嗯，这不是我。”而我会说：“好吧，你先从‘这不是我’这句话开始说起。” 当你真正成为领导者时，你肯定做得对了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What was the process like for you to work through that? You said it took a long time. What made it effective for you? Was there a coach involved? Something else?
turns.zh: 克服这些挑战的过程是怎样的？你说这花了很长时间。是什么让你最终取得成效？当时有导师指导吗？还有其他因素吗？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I got a lot of setback. I get a lot of negative feedback. I had a lot of abrupt challenges at work where folks would say, "You're not collaborating well. Your peers don't have the same level of respect as they should." And I was like, "Are you kidding me? That's not who I am. These things that are being said about are completely ironic." I was very much struggling and that's when I said, "You know what? I can struggle and blame others, but what if they were right? I'm going to be doing this for 30 more years, it's kind of worth it to figure out if they're right. If they're wrong, then you don't lose." And that's what kind of forced it. And then the tooling starts, then you start talking through. My self-awareness was strong enough that I was able to say, "Okay, now I understand it." I had some peer feedback that helped bring it home from someone I trusted. So that was a kind of linchpin to this, but these are tough, tough things to break through. And oftentimes they don't come nicely, I guess, is the point.
turns.zh: 我遇到了很多挫折，收到了大量负面反馈。工作中也遇到过突然的挑战，比如有人说：“你不善于团队协作，同事们对你的尊重程度不够。”我当时就想：“开什么玩笑？这根本不是我啊！这些指责简直荒谬至极。” 我深陷困境，这时我才意识到：“我可以继续抱怨他人，但万一他们说得对呢？我还要继续工作30年，现在花时间弄清楚他们是否正确也不算亏。如果他们错了，那也没什么损失。” 这才迫使我改变了态度。接下来开始反思工具运用，剖析自身问题。我的自我认知足够清晰，能及时领悟问题所在。同时，我信任的同事给予的反馈也让我豁然开朗。这正是关键所在，但要突破这些难题实在不易。很多时候，突破并非易事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was going to ask what that turning point for you was, and it sounds like it was direct feedback from someone you really trusted that's like, "Oh, I really need to take this seriously."
turns.zh: 我想问的是，你的转折点是什么？听起来像是来自你信任之人的直接反馈，让你意识到必须认真对待这些问题。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: You got it. You got it. Because I had a lot of feedback that I was dismissing and then I had feedback from someone, I'm like, "That person I should listen to because they're giving me the feedback for the right reasons and they have the right language."
turns.zh: 没错，确实如此。因为我之前忽视了很多反馈，而这次得到的反馈来自值得信赖的人，他们给出的建议合理，措辞得当。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Comes back to the power of getting feedback and getting good at that.
turns.zh: 这再次印证了获得反馈并善于利用反馈的力量。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: And making people feel safe and giving it.
turns.zh: 还有营造安全的反馈环境，坦诚地给予反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm. That's a good segue to maybe the last question. You told me once that a lot of the people that you work with that have kind of made it have a lot of mental health challenges, that they didn't expect their life to be the way it is necessarily when they got there. Can you just talk about what you see there in that group?
turns.zh: 嗯，这为最后一个问题做了很好的铺垫。你曾告诉我，在你共事过的人中，很多成功者都曾面临心理健康问题，他们并未预料到自己的生活会如此艰难。能否谈谈这个群体的情况？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah. This is a story that I don't think is told very well right now, and partly because it's such a luxury problem, it's almost a little embarrassing to discuss it openly as so many people struggle with so many basic needs, going through layoffs, going through all these challenges. I mean, these are real issues. But I think that what I've noticed is that if you kind of break career as we've done in this podcast between sort of act one, act two and act three, if act one is sort of learning and being that sort of builder and then maybe building the car, and then act two is building the factory, act three is like, what's after that? What do you do after that? And I think that act three in the past wasn't as long as it is now. Before, people would proverbially retire in their 60s when they used to actually physically work.
turns.zh: 是的。这个话题目前讨论得不多，一部分原因是这属于奢侈的问题，公开谈论时甚至有些尴尬，毕竟很多人还在为基本生存挣扎，应对裁员、各种挑战。这些才是实实在在的问题。但我发现，如果把职业生涯按三幕剧划分——第一幕是学习、搭建框架，第二幕是建造工厂，第三幕是超越现有——现在第三幕的时间拉得太长了。过去人们60岁退休，那时确实还在体力劳动。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Now almost all your listeners sit at a desk all day, so they don't need to retire by any means. And health is getting better. You might see folks work until their 70s or 80s. So that means that their careers are potentially 60 years long. So even if you're 20 years or 30 years in your career, you're only halfway through. So this act three could be a thing. And I don't think we talk about act three enough. What often happens is, and this is what I've been watching for people that are at my age, is they sort of succeed and then they become lost. They almost goes hand in hand.
turns.zh: 如今，几乎所有听众每天都坐在办公桌前工作，因此他们根本无需退休。人们的健康状况也日益改善，你可能会看到有些人工作到70岁或80岁。这意味着他们的职业生涯可能长达60年。即便你已在职场打拼了20年或30年，也不过才走了一半路程。所以第三幕的人生可能正在上演。但我们对此谈论得实在太少了。现实情况是——以我这个年龄段的人为例——他们往往事业有成后却迷失了方向。这种现象往往相伴而生。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: So when I was a kid and I was growing up in the Midwest, entertainment was going to the dog tracks, and not even the horse tracks, we didn't have horses. So it was the greyhound dog tracks. So people would bet on a dog and greyhound would go around the ring and then you would see. I bet on number three and I'll make a buck or something. The way that they motivated the dogs was they had these fake rabbits, which sounds kind of cruel and horrible, so I don't want the SPCA to come after you. But the point is that they'd have these fake rabbits. And what was interesting is, the moment that the dogs, if they accidentally touched the rabbit, the sort of the tail because the machine broke, because these tails would go around faster than the dogs, which would then motivate the dogs to go around in circles. Sometimes the machines would break, the dogs would actually catch the rabbit, they would never run again.
turns.zh: 我童年生活在中西部地区，那时的娱乐活动就是去赛狗场，甚至连赛马场都没有——我们这儿没有马。所以人们会赌狗比赛。灰狗会在赛道上奔跑，而你只需押注数字3就能赢钱。当时驱动狗狗跑圈的工具是假兔子。这听起来残忍又可怕，我可不想让动物保护协会找上门来。但关键是，狗狗一旦不小心碰到兔子尾巴（因为机器故障导致尾巴转速比狗跑得快），就会被激发跑圈。有时机器出故障，狗狗真把兔子抓住了，那它们就再也跑不动了。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: The reason why they wouldn't run again is because there was like, "Well, what's next? I've achieved what I was looking for." So I think this happens a ton. It's like, your listeners are spending time focused on like, "Well, one day I will be X. I will be that vice president. I will have more money. I will have built something. I will have started a company." But they don't think about what happens next, and when it happens, when they succeed, their North Star, their entire way of wiring their career, themselves, it has been around getting to that place. And I think that if you're going to get there 30 years in and you have a 60-year career, a lot of the discussion I've been having with myself and with others has been, you probably need to start working on that North Star now.
turns.zh: 它们不再跑动的原因在于：“好吧，下一步该做什么？我已经达成了目标。”这种情况屡见不鲜。听众们往往专注于某个目标，比如“总有一天我会成为副总裁，赚大钱，开创事业”，但他们从不思考下一步该做什么。当成功来临时，支撑他们职业生涯的北极星已然消逝。我认为，如果你在30年后才意识到自己还有60年的职业生涯，那么我和他人一直在探讨的问题是：你或许需要从现在开始规划那个北极星。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: What's the second thing? What's your career next look like? How do you ensure that you are always going to have something important and motivating to do with your career? Otherwise, you'll keep working because you had no nothing else to do, but you'll be sadder, or you'll find ways to create war when peace is needed, or you'll spend money in an attempt to earn more, or you'll find habits that are bad. And I really want us to have long 60-year, 70-year careers, not just 30-year or 10-year, which is why I enter this into the vocabulary out there.
turns.zh: 第二件事是什么？你的职业生涯接下来会怎样？如何确保职业生涯中始终有重要且激励人心的事物？否则，你会因为无事可做而继续工作，但你会变得更沮丧，或是在需要和平时制造战争，或是试图用钱来赚更多钱，又或是养成坏习惯。我真心希望我们能拥有60年、70年的漫长职业生涯，而非仅仅30年或10年。这也是我将此观点纳入公众讨论的原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really resonating with me. I had a similar experience. I had a startup, and my whole goal was just like, "I just want to start a company." That's my goal. That's all I got in life. I want to start a company and then maybe sell it, maybe go somewhere with it. So I did and then we sold it to Airbnb and then I got to Airbnb and I was just like, "What the hell do I do now? I don't have any other goals." And it was pretty sad. Exactly how you're describing. It was just like, "I guess I'll just work here and I don't know, maybe I'll start another company, but I already did the thing I wanted to do."
turns.zh: 这真的让我深有共鸣。我也有过类似的经历。我曾创办过一家初创公司，当时我的全部目标就是“我只想创办一家公司”。这就是我的目标。这是我人生中唯一的追求——创办一家公司，然后或许将其出售，或许让它有所发展。所以我做到了，但后来我们把公司卖给了Airbnb。加入Airbnb后，我陷入了迷茫：“现在该做什么？我没有其他目标了。”这感觉太糟糕了，就像你描述的那样。当时我就像在说：“看来我只能在这里工作了，或许再创办一家公司，但我已经完成了想做的事。”

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Your story is I think very inspiring because what you did is you said, "I think the thing that I want to do is give, but I want to do it in my own way and I want to create something, but I want to do something that I think I can do for 30 years and I want to do it." It has lots and lots of spokes to it. So you reinvented yourself professionally, but you created a new North Star.
turns.zh: 你的故事我觉得非常鼓舞人心，因为你做到了：你说“我想做的事就是奉献，但要用自己的方式；要创造些东西，但要能坚持30年；还要有清晰的方向。”这里面有很多层面的思考。所以你重新塑造了自己的职业生涯，找到了新的北极星。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: My sense is, for every one of you, Lenny, there's a hundred that could do that, that could do giving, that could do things that could scale, but that end up falling into what got them to be successful in act two and they get stuck. So this is the reason why when you hit your skip, keep looking for the next skip, is the point I'm trying to make. And I think you're an inspiration for a lot of folks who have seen you transition and realizes life after just being a tech professional entrepreneur, there's got to be ways to do more of this for all of your listeners. And I think it's never too early to start thinking through. It's actually quite powering to think that you have such a long career. You can make mistakes and you can do some amazing things down the road.
turns.zh: 我的感觉是，莱尼，你这样的人还有成百上千个，他们也想奉献，也想做能扩展规模的事，但最终却陷入了成功后的第二幕，停滞不前。这就是为什么当你遇到瓶颈时，要继续寻找下一个突破口，这就是我想传达的观点。你对许多见证了你转型、意识到科技专业人士创业后生活可以更多元的人来说，是个激励。其实永远不嫌早开始思考这些问题。意识到自己职业生涯漫长，这其实很赋能。你可以犯错，也能在未来创造惊人成就。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. This is my fourth career, is what I realized. I was a engineer, then a founder, then a product manager, and now whatever this is.
turns.zh: 是啊。我意识到这是我的第四次职业转型了。我曾是工程师，后来是创始人，再后来是产品经理，现在也不知道算什么了。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Whatever this is.
turns.zh: 也不知道算什么了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Whatever this is. I guess, just to give people something inspiring, productive, what are maybe some examples of North Stars you've seen that people can evolve into? I guess one path is this path of content creation, helping people learn stuff. What else have you seen that might work out for people?
turns.zh: 也不知道算什么了。我想给人们一些鼓舞人心、富有成效的建议，也许能举几个北极星的例子，让大家有所启发？我猜一条路是内容创作，帮助人们学习知识。还有什么路径可能适合人们呢？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I think that all variations here come into two categories. One categories are ways to drive more scaled economics. I've made millions. My North Star is to now make it tens. I've made tens. My North star is to do hundreds. That's what drives people from, it's not entrepreneurship, it's investing; it's not investing, it's private equity, et cetera. Whether we describe that as a bad quest or a good quest is a decision for your listener. The other arc is around giving. Eastern philosophies that have been around for thousands of years talk about this as the sort of end state of happiness. I think that maybe to be provocative, I think that it's okay for you in act one and act two to not predicate yourself around the notion of giving to others because this is maybe the time on the planet where you need to take and you need to create.
turns.zh: 我认为这里所有的变体都分两类。一类是如何推动更大规模的经济效益。我赚了数百万。我的北极星是现在赚几千万。我赚了几千万。我的北极星是赚几亿。这推动着人们从创业转向投资，从投资转向私募股权等等。我们是否认为这是好是坏的追求，由听众自己判断。另一条路径是关于奉献。几千年来的东方哲学都把这视为幸福的终极状态。我想说，也许有点冒犯，但在第一幕和第二幕，你没必要把自己局限于奉献他人之类的概念，因为这或许是我们在地球上需要索取和创造的时期。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: But boy, if you're going to work on an act three and you have 30 years, regardless of where you are economically, if you feel like you can take that off the table, if you can find ways to give, whatever that means to you, however that translates to you, is that content, is that volunteer, is that starting a company that is more mission based, that is not my role, but I think that if you are able to do that for 30 years and be giving, not only is that going to be more fulfilling than your act one and act two, but it's tremendous for society, very empowering. And that's where I commend you because you're giving through your passion but also making a livelihood. And I think that that's a very powerful blend that is hard to achieve in act one and act two given constraints. And that's the liberation that act three provides.
turns.zh: 天哪，如果你要迎来第三幕人生，并且你还有30年的时间——无论你的经济状况如何，如果你觉得自己能放下这些顾虑，如果你能找到奉献的方式，无论这对你的意义是什么，无论它如何转化为行动——无论是志愿服务，还是创办一项更具使命感的公司——这都不是我的角色。但我认为，如果你能在30年里奉献自己，不仅会比前两幕人生更有成就感，还能为社会带来巨大价值，极具赋能意义。这正是值得赞赏的地方，因为你既在追随自己的热情，又能谋生糊口。这是第一幕和第二幕中难以实现的强大融合，也是第三幕所带来的解放。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you think your act three plus ends up being?
turns.zh: 你觉得自己的第三幕人生会是什么样的？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Many have asked me about this. I would say that I'll use the word, and then I'll tell you I won't use that word. So it is around my passion around coaching and giving to others. But because I'm a product person, because I've seen success in building products, thinking about scale, thinking about community, I definitively plan to devote my act three towards coaching and giving to others and lifting up those that with the right advice at the right time can change their trajectory. But scaling that and doing that in a way that is very authentic is really the hardest part and it's product problem. So that's what I'll devote 30 years to and I look forward to that every day.
turns.zh: 很多人问过我这个问题。我会先说一个词，然后告诉你我不会用这个词。总之，围绕我的热情——教练和帮助他人——展开。但因为我曾是产品人，因为我在产品开发、规模化思维和社区建设方面取得过成功，我绝对计划将第三幕人生投入到教练和帮助他人，以及提升那些在正确的时间获得正确建议就能改变轨迹的人。但以真实的方式实现规模化推广才是最难的部分，这是一个产品难题。所以这就是我未来30年要致力于的方向，我每天都对此充满期待。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is beautiful. That feels like an exactly correct fit for you, and I'm here to help you on that journey any way I can.
turns.zh: 这太棒了。这感觉和你完美契合，我会尽一切可能在这条道路上支持你。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Thank you, my friend.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，我的朋友。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. Is there anything else you wanted to touch on before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 当然。还有什么想补充的吗？我们即将进入激动人心的闪电问答环节。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: No, I just appreciate your genuine offer to have me attend and participate in this wonderful podcast that you created.
turns.zh: 没有了。我只想感谢你真诚地邀请我参加并参与你创建的这个精彩播客。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's absolutely my pleasure. And it's not over yet. We've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got six questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 那真是我的荣幸。不过还没结束呢。我们现在要进入激动人心的闪电问答环节。我有六个问题要问你，准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I am ready.
turns.zh: 我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 你向别人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: So two, and both business books. Sorry, I'm going to come across boring. But one is this sort of little bit of an old school book called Crossing the Chasm by Geoffrey Moore. I don't know if other speakers have spoken about this, but it's a book that Geoffrey Moore wrote, and it's a book that really talks about how to get your first product on base. So it's this concept of creating a beachhead. I like that concept. Marketing is something that we don't talk about in enough and product.
turns.zh: 两本，都是商业书籍。抱歉，可能听起来有点无聊。但第一本是杰夫·摩尔的《跨越鸿沟》。这本书讲如何让你的第一款产品站稳脚跟。这本书提到了创建滩头阵地的概念。我很喜欢这个概念。营销是我们在产品领域谈论得不够的话题。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: And then the second one is a book that none of your listeners have actually probably heard of called Leadership and Self-Deception. It's a six-hour audio that I highly recommend. It's a story about a person who has hit a wall and who's getting all this feedback that they don't know what to make of, and it's around their mindset being stuck in a box. That was very powerful when I listened to it in my late 20s. So I encourage all of your listeners to grab that one. It's not one that anyone normally would hit, but it's a fun story. It's a good ride, and I think maybe you'll get something out of it.
turns.zh: 接下来是第二本书，叫《领导力与自我欺骗》（Leadership and Self-Deception）。这是一本时长六小时的有声书，我强烈推荐。它讲述了一个遭遇瓶颈的人的故事，他收到了各种反馈却不知如何应对，核心问题在于思维被困在固有框架中。我在20多岁时听这本书时，深有共鸣。所以我鼓励所有听众去听听。这本书可能不是大家通常会接触到的，但它是个有趣的故事，值得一听。我相信你们也能从中收获不少。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have not heard of that second one. I'm excited to check it out. I have Crossing the Chasm back behind me on that shelf somewhere. And you talk about how marketing isn't something product leaders and managers think about enough, and I have many marketing-oriented guests on this podcast and those episodes do the least well, but I'm just going to keep doing it because I totally agree with you. I think there's so much to learn from marketing. It's connected to growth, which is connected to product. So I agree.
turns.zh: 我没听过第二本。我很期待去看看。我记得《跨越鸿沟》（Crossing the Chasm）还在我书架上某个角落落灰。你提到产品领导者和经理们往往不重视营销，我在播客上请过很多营销相关的嘉宾，但那些集数的收听量最差。不过我还是会继续邀请，因为我完全赞同你的观点。营销领域有太多值得学习的地方，它与增长息息相关，而增长又与产品紧密相连。所以我完全同意你的看法。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah, and I think that marketing is a language of connecting products with people. That is what a product manager does, but we often lack the language. We lack the thinking around how to explain it, and yet we spend all our time on data and features for that. The diversity of having both playbooks can make one of just a much more powerful builder. So I agree with you. Marketing folks is probably some of the best content and the least listen to. So maybe that's a plug for people to go back to those episodes.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为营销是连接产品与用户的语言。这正是产品经理的职责所在，但我们往往缺乏这方面的语言。我们缺乏如何解释的思维框架，却把所有精力都投入到数据和功能上。拥有这两种思维模式的人会成为更强大的建设者。所以我完全赞同你的观点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 100%. That's what everyone should do. I don't know if you know this, but actually, at Airbnb, the product manager function has been renamed to product marketing. So all the product managers are product marketers because Brian is so big on, you're not just building product, your job is also to make sure people use it. We'll see how that experiment goes, but that's a bold move I thought.
turns.zh: 完全同意。这正是每个人应该做的。你可能不知道，Airbnb实际上已经把产品经理的职位更名为产品营销了。所以所有的产品经理都成了产品营销师，因为布莱恩（Brian）非常强调，产品开发不只是建造产品，你的工作还包括确保人们会使用它。我们拭目以待这个实验的效果，但我认为这是一个大胆的尝试。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Very much so. Very much. But it's an homage to this concept.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。完全赞同。但这也是对这个理念的致敬。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Exactly. Okay, back to landing ground. What is a favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 没错，回归正题。最近你最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I'm a huge sports fan, so I have tickets to the Warriors and 49ers, and I am a big Bay Area sports fan. Giannis is my son's favorite player. He's a basketball player for the Milwaukee Bucks, and they have this Disney+ story called the Rise story, and it's a story about his childhood and how he struggled to find notoriety and how he made it into the professional leagues. It's a great Disney+ family show and it's a great kind of zero to hero type thing. So I love that story.
turns.zh: 我是个体育迷，所以我有勇士队和49人队的票，也是湾区体育迷。扬尼斯（Giannis）是我儿子最喜欢的球员。他是密尔沃基雄鹿队的篮球运动员，迪士尼+上有一部关于他的纪录片《崛起》（The Rise），讲述了他童年时期如何努力获得关注并最终进入职业联赛的故事。这是一部很棒的迪士尼+家庭剧，也是从零到英雄的典型故事。所以我很喜欢这个故事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like you're going to have a really good answer to this next one. What is a favorite interview question that you like to ask?
turns.zh: 我觉得你对下一个问题会有很棒的答案。你最喜欢问哪个面试问题？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I like the format of, what's something that everyone takes for granted that you think is essentially hogwash or inaccurate? Sometimes I'll ask a manager, "Look, you've managed hundreds of people in your career, what's conventional wisdom that you bet against that you have found is actually inaccurate?" And you can do that for what do people think about AI, that's inaccurate, that everyone believes you could do that for domains, you can do all kinds of things.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这种形式——有没有什么大家习以为常但你认为根本是胡说八道或不准确的东西？有时我会问经理：“看，你职业生涯里管理过数百人，对于那些被公认的‘传统智慧’，你有没有反其道而行之、发现其不准确的例子？”你也可以用这个方法来探讨人们对AI的看法——那些错误观点，以及人们认为你能做到的各种事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. Is there something you specifically look for there, or is it just depends on what you hear?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个做法。你有没有特别关注的点？还是说只是看别人怎么回答？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I'm always looking for people to break this sort of interview mindset. Everyone always prepares for interviews and then their entire conversation is predicting what you think you want me to say. And as a result, you can have high-quality people that you dismiss because they weren't genuine. There's no way to answer that question without being genuinely opinionated because it starts with, "What is the thing that you think I want to say here? And then tell me why it's inaccurate." So when I break that wall, I'm testing, is this person authentic? Because sometimes I'm dismissing them because they told me nothing new, but I don't want the interview process to penalize them. And this was my save question, but I can't use it now that I've told everyone.
turns.zh: 我总是在寻找能打破这种面试思维定式的人。当人们为面试做准备后，整个对话过程都是在预测你想听什么答案。结果，可能有很多高质量的候选人被淘汰了，只因为他们不够真诚。要回答这个问题，就必须保持真实的观点，因为问题开头就是：“你觉得我在这里想听什么？然后告诉我为什么它不准确。” 所以当我打破这种隔阂时，我是在测试这个人是否真实可信？因为有时我会因为他们没有提供新观点而淘汰他们，但我不想让面试过程惩罚他们。这原本是我准备的救场问题，但现在已经告诉大家了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's going to be all over TikTok soon. Everyone's going to know this. Next question, what's a favorite recent product that you've discovered that you love?
turns.zh: 这很快就会在TikTok上疯传了。大家都会知道这个问题。下一个问题，近期你发现的最喜欢的产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: The geeky answer in me is the Arc Browser, which I think probably a lot of folks are starting to use and your listeners. Part of the reason is, I think it's just great for folks that have hundreds of tabs, and if you work at a scaled organization, you just have lots of tabs. But I think it's also, as a product guy, I thought Chrome was pretty good. They've got gajillions of people using it and billions of installs. So at some point, you kind of come to the conclusion that this is probably good enough. And then you see a product obviously built with a much smaller team and you're like, "Huh, there actually is opportunities to innovate." And any time you see a innovation on something that's mature, as a product person, I think that's just fascinating. And I was just blown away at how they created something that's better than something I hold as a true set.
turns.zh: 作为一个极客，我推荐Arc浏览器。我觉得很多听众可能也开始用了。部分原因是，对于有数百个标签页的人来说（如果你在大公司工作，就会有很多标签页）它太棒了。但作为产品经理，我之前觉得Chrome已经足够好了。毕竟有数十亿用户在使用。于是你会得出结论，Chrome已经足够好了。但当你看到一个由小团队打造的产品时，你会感叹：“哇，原来还有创新空间。”每当看到成熟产品中的创新时，作为产品经理，我觉得这太迷人了。Arc浏览器让我惊叹不已，它比我心目中的标准产品还要出色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. We had Josh on the podcast, we talked about a lot of their philosophies. And on the tab thing, I think the key there is it closes your tabs after 24 hours unless you put them in a specific place, which I love because I was like, you think you would do that, but you don't. And then it's broke so beautiful, you wake up in the morning, everything's gone, but you can save stuff that you want. The other thing I'll mention with Arc, by the way, also huge fan, that's all I use, and I'm not an investor, just a fan, is the onboarding experience is the best onboarding experience I've seen. I was just like, I did it and I got a tweet about this. This is so good. And actually, if you go to that episode, there's a link to get past the wait list and just-
turns.zh: 是的。我们在播客上邀请了Josh，讨论了很多他们的理念。关于标签页的问题，我认为关键在于24小时后会关闭标签页，除非你把它们存放在特定位置。这点我很喜欢，因为我觉得大家会想当然地认为自己会这么做，但其实不会。然后它又设计得非常贴心，早上醒来时所有数据都消失了，但你可以保存想保存的内容。顺便说一句，关于Arc浏览器，我也是忠实用户——虽然我不是投资者，只是粉丝——它的入门体验是我见过最好的。我用过后收到推特反馈，真是太棒了。实际上如果你去看那期播客，有链接可以跳过等待名单，直接——

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Oh, that's right. Yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，对了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. You gave me many thousands of invites. Okay, keep going. What is something relatively minor you've changed in the way you develop products and your team that's had a big impact on the team's ability to execute?
turns.zh: 是的。你给了我几千份邀请函。好的，继续说。你在产品开发和团队管理方面做过哪些相对微小的调整，却对团队执行能力产生了重大影响？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: A little bit of this is just because of scale, but oftentimes we think a lot about the products and the features and the decisions that we're working on, and then we think that meetings are a nuisance or a must-have necessary evil to be able to deliver. Sometimes I realize that at a scaled organization, the meeting operating system is as important as the products that we're building because it sort of speaks to how we scale and how we ensure we have the right degree of delegation, the right conversations, and then the right acceleration on the right decisions.
turns.zh: 这其中一部分只是因为规模效应，但很多时候，我们对正在开发的产品、功能和决策思考良多，然后又觉得会议是件烦人的事，或者是必须完成的必要之恶。有时我意识到，在一个规模化组织中，会议运作体系与我们正在开发的产品同样重要，因为它关乎我们如何实现规模化，以及如何确保有适当的授权、开展有效的讨论，并最终在正确的决策上达成共识。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: So what's interesting is every quarter, in my current teams, even in my past teams, I talk about our meetings like a product. We're on version seven in my team, and so we're like, "Hey, version seven, every 90 days, these are the meetings, these are the discussions, this is how we organize, these are the attendees, and then here's how we make decisions. This is the cadence of the week. This is when people can work from home, hybrid, whatever it might be." And then I take feedback two months in and then every three months we make another route.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，在我目前所在的团队，甚至是我过去的团队，每个季度我都会把会议当作产品来谈论。我们团队现在已经到了第七个版本了，所以我们会说：“嘿，第七个版本，每90天，这些是会议，这些是讨论，这样组织，参与人员是这些，然后是如何做出决策。每周的节奏是这样的。人们可以在家工作、采用混合办公模式，随心所欲。”然后每两个月收集反馈，再每三个月调整一次流程。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: What it finds is that people then can plan and they can make meeting time effective. And meeting time is such precious time. It's the most expensive time in a company. So when I was in a startup, I couldn't imagine doing this, but now this is like my bread and butter as a leader. It's the process part. And frankly, for new folks that are new in leadership positions in a new company, it's the one thing you can do when you have low context. When you don't know how the product works, you can look at things with fresh eyes and see inefficiencies when everyone that's been in the system can't see it. I'm a huge fan of rebooting meetings first. So process first, then people, then product, then strategy is sort of the notion I make, and this is this first thing I always do.
turns.zh: 结果发现，这样一来，人们就能提前规划，让会议时间变得高效。会议时间非常宝贵，是公司里最昂贵的资源。所以当我在初创公司时，根本想象不到能做这种事，但现在这成了我作为领导者的核心工作。这是流程层面的东西。坦白说，对于新公司中初担领导重任的人来说，当你对产品运作机制知之甚少时，就能以全新的视角发现低效率之处，而那些深陷其中的人却视而不见。我特别推崇先从重启会议入手。流程优先，然后是人才，最后是产品和战略，这就是我的理念，也是我首先要做的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question, what is one thing every PM listening should do to help their career?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题，每个听众都应该做些什么来助力自己的职业发展？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Ensure that the story you will tell about the work you're doing today is meaningful for your skip job. So if you sit down and you write down, "In six months, in 12 months, in 24 months, when I achieve or finish this role, here's the paragraph I'll write. Here's a problem I solved. Here's the skill I built. Here's the headwind I faced. Here's what I did to overcome it." Use I in the sentence, do not use we. We will do good things. You are who we are thinking about, your career. We're not looking for we. Master the story now. Understand the story. If the story sucks, you probably should be thinking through how to make the story not suck. But that to me is a very good career decision and I think everyone is building their story today. I want to know that story. I want that story to be incredibly compelling because whether you promote it or not, that story's compelling. You'll be promoted in career. And that's what we're here for.
turns.zh: 要确保你讲述的当前工作故事对你的下一个职位有意义。比如，如果你坐下来写下：“六个月后，十二个月后，二十四个月后，当我完成或结束这个角色时，我会写下这样的段落。我解决了这个问题。我培养了这项技能。我面对了这样的挑战，我是这样克服它的。”在句子中用“我”而不是“我们”。我们会做好事，但我们关注的是你——你的职业生涯。我们不是在寻找“我们”。现在就掌握这个故事。理解这个故事。如果故事很糟糕，你就该想办法让它不糟糕了。但对我来说，这是一个非常明智的职业决策，我相信每个人今天都在构建自己的故事。我想了解这个故事。我希望这个故事极具吸引力，因为无论你是否主动推广，这个故事都会引人入胜。你会因此获得晋升。这就是我们在这里的意义所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Nikhyl, this is the first time we've ever met. I'm such a fan instantly. This might be my new favorite episode. I'm so excited for people to listen to this. There's so much value here. Two final questions before we wrap up. Where can folks find you online if they want to learn more? And also, talk about maybe various community, The Skip, and all that stuff that people can check out. And then how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 尼基尔，这是我们第一次见面。我一下子就成了你的粉丝。这可能是我最喜欢的一期节目了。我特别期待大家能来收听，内容太有价值了。在结束前再问两个问题。如果想了解更多信息，人们可以在哪里找到你？另外，能否谈谈社区The Skip以及相关资源？最后，听众如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I'm building this brand around The Skip because I'm so passionate. There's two outlets that people can easily connect. One is the podcast, which much like yourselves is available on Apple and Spotify and others. So I'd love for people to join my podcast and hear. What I'm now moving my podcast to is almost like coaching calls. Because I have so many of them, I'm saying like, "Hey, 30 minutes, let me walk you through a problem and hear how I'm thinking about it, whether that's a transition discussion or compensation discussion, et cetera." And then the other one is this sort of newsletter that I have on Substack, which is a bit of a mirror of the podcast. It's different forms of the same topic areas. So, would love for your listeners to connect with that.
turns.zh: 我围绕The Skip打造这个品牌，因为我对它充满热情。大家可以通过两个平台与我互动。首先是播客，和你们的播客一样，可以在Apple和Spotify等平台收听。我希望听众能订阅我的播客，收听内容。现在我的播客逐渐转向类似指导通话的形式。我每周会接到很多这样的请求，比如“30分钟带你分析一个问题，探讨转型策略或薪酬谈判等”。另外，我在Substack上推出了同名新闻通讯，内容与播客类似，只是形式有所不同。欢迎听众关注。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I think as far as getting in touch with me, LinkedIn is where I spend most of my time professionally. So between Twitter and LinkedIn, my presence is relatively easy to find. And then how listeners can help me, I mean, one, you can build the most fulfilling career story and be your best, but also give back and pull others forward. Whether that's through your act three or whether that's just helping others, I mean, I think that would be the most fulfilling to me. I think feedback from your listeners to me on things they wish I would spend time talking about is incredibly empowering for my content because then I can deliver more meaningful content. It's very different from yours, but I think it's all around the arc of trying to help people gain forward and be more effective tech professionals. So I would love to hear from your listeners.
turns.zh: 关于联系我的方式，LinkedIn是我工作中最常用的平台。Twitter和LinkedIn都能轻松找到我。听众如何提供帮助呢？首先，你可以打造最充实的职业生涯故事，成就更好的自己，同时回馈社会，帮助他人。无论是通过第三幕规划，还是直接助人，我相信这才是最有意义的。听众对我分享的内容反馈，对我创作很有启发，能让我提供更有价值的素材。虽然风格和你们不同，但核心都是帮助人们成长，成为更高效的技术人才。我期待听众的反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to make sure people know where to go to do this. For feedback, do you recommend LinkedIn?
turns.zh: 确保大家知道反馈渠道在哪里。建议用LinkedIn吗？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah, LinkedIn is the ideal, but you can also find me on Twitter if you are just trying to add a quick... If you're trying to follow me, follow me on LinkedIn. If you're looking for feedback, just tweet me.
turns.zh: 是的，LinkedIn最方便，但Twitter也可以快速添加关注。想反馈的话，就发推给我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then for The Skip newsletter, what is the URL to go check that out?
turns.zh: The Skip新闻通讯的网址是什么？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: It's theskip.substack.com.
turns.zh: theskip.substack.com。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And you don't publish often, but each issue is incredibly valuable, so we'll definitely link to that all in the show notes. Nikhyl, thank you again so much for being here. I will let you go now. This was amazing.
turns.zh: 太棒了。你不常发布，但每期内容都极具价值，我们一定会在节目笔记中附上链接。尼基尔，再次感谢你的到来。这次交流太棒了。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah, thank you, Lenny. Appreciate it.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，莱尼。很感激。

turns.en: Bye, everyone.
turns.zh: 再见，各位。
